Mercury also offers an insured cash sweep product that spreads deposits across partner banks to increase FDIC coverage, and a treasury product that invests idle cash in money market funds for companies with larger balances and a longer cash runway. Each of these has its own minimums and eligibility conditions, which vary by product and have changed over time.

Payments cover most of what an operating company needs. Domestic wires and ACH transfers are free and unlimited, which is the single most cited reason startups move to Mercury, since traditional banks often charge per outgoing wire. International wires are supported in many currencies at rates that are generally more favourable than a retail bank's, though a fee applies and the amount depends on currency and destination. Bill pay lets a company schedule and approve vendor payments, and Mercury can issue checks and pay by card where a vendor requires it. There is no support for depositing physical cash, which is a hard constraint for cash-heavy businesses.

Cards include virtual and physical debit cards tied to the checking accounts, with per-card spending limits, the ability to lock or close a card instantly, and integration into the wider expense workflow. Mercury also offers a business credit card that underwrites against the company's financial position, with no annual fee and cash back on spend. Because credit limits are set from company data rather than a personal guarantee, eligibility depends on cash balance, revenue and runway, and early-stage companies without meaningful balances may not qualify or may receive modest limits.

Finance operations tooling is where Mercury differentiates from a neobank that only offers accounts. Multi-user access comes with granular permissions, so a bookkeeper can view and categorise transactions without being able to send money, and an approver can release payments above a threshold. Approval workflows can require more than one signature for transfers over a defined amount. Accounting sync pushes transactions and receipts into QuickBooks Online and Xero, and Mercury's own categorisation reduces the manual coding burden. Audit logs record who did what and when, which matters as soon as a company has a board, an auditor or an acquisition on the horizon.

Mercury also addresses the funding side of a startup's finances. It maintains relationships with venture lenders and can introduce companies to debt facilities, and its treasury management is designed for the specific problem of a large funding round landing in one account. For a company that has just raised, spreading deposits across insured programme banks and earning yield on the remainder is a practical risk control rather than an investment strategy.

Commercial terms are the most attractive part of the proposition for many buyers. There is no monthly fee for the core business accounts, no minimum balance to keep the account open and no charge for domestic wires or ACH. Fees apply to international wires, certain expedited transfers and specific products. Mercury's revenue comes from interchange on card spend, from fees on international payments and from the spread on cash management products. Where a minimum balance or a fee does apply, it attaches to the optional treasury and sweep products rather than to basic banking, and the current figures for those products should be confirmed on Mercury's own pricing page because they are revised as interest rates and partner terms change.

Against Brex and Ramp, Mercury is banking-first rather than card-first. It offers real deposit accounts, free domestic wires and cash management, and its card and expense features are lighter than what those two platforms provide. Many companies run Mercury as their bank and Brex or Ramp as their spend platform, which is a combination both vendors tacitly accept. Against a traditional bank such as Silicon Valley Bank or a regional commercial bank, Mercury is cheaper, faster to open and better integrated with accounting software, but it lacks branches, lacks relationship-based lending and lacks the depth of treasury services a large company needs. Against other fintech banks such as Relay, Mercury is stronger on venture-scale cash management and weaker on features aimed at smaller cash-based businesses.

The limitations are worth listing before signing up. Mercury requires a US business entity in most cases, and it does not accept sole proprietorships without a registered company. It declines or restricts certain industries, including adult content, gambling, cannabis, some cryptocurrency activity, money transmission and other high-risk categories. There is no cash deposit capability and no branch access. Credit products are limited and are not a substitute for a bank line of credit. Support is digital-first, and while it is generally well regarded, there is no in-person escalation path. Account opening involves identity and beneficial ownership verification that can take days when documentation is incomplete, and accounts can be closed if activity falls outside the acceptable use policy.

Mercury fits US-incorporated startups, software companies, e-commerce businesses, agencies and holding companies that operate online, move money by wire and ACH frequently, and want free domestic transfers plus multi-user controls with accounting sync. It does not fit sole proprietors, businesses in restricted industries, cash-heavy retailers, companies that need branch banking or traditional commercial lending, and non-US entities without a qualifying structure. When comparing alternatives, Mercury is the strongest choice for a startup's primary operating bank, Brex and Ramp are the stronger choices for card controls and spend management on top of it, and a traditional commercial bank remains necessary once a company needs credit facilities, treasury services at scale or in-person relationship banking.

name: Expensify
description: Expensify automates expense reporting through SmartScan receipt capture, credit card reconciliation, and approval workflows. Adds corporate cards, invoicing, multi-currency reimbursement, and travel booking through Expensify Travel.
overview:
Expensify is an expense management platform built around receipt capture, reimbursement and corporate card reconciliation. It was founded in 2009, which makes it one of the longest-established products in the category, and it became a publicly traded company on the Nasdaq in 2021. The core proposition has not changed much: an employee photographs a receipt, Expensify extracts the merchant, date, amount and currency, the expense joins a report, the report clears an approval chain, and the money is reimbursed or reconciled against a card statement. What has changed is the surrounding platform, which now includes a corporate card, bill payments, invoicing and travel booking. It serves freelancers at one end and multinational companies with employees in many countries at the other.

SmartScan is the receipt engine and the reason most companies evaluate Expensify first. A receipt can be captured by photographing it in the mobile app, forwarding it to a dedicated Expensify email address, or uploading a batch of images or PDFs from a desktop. Extraction identifies the vendor and amount, detects the currency and applies the exchange rate, and proposes a category based on the merchant and the user's history. Expensify advertises a very high accuracy rate for printed receipts in supported languages, and the failure mode in practice is crumpled thermal paper, handwritten notes and unusual international formats rather than ordinary restaurant or fuel receipts. Extraction happens asynchronously, so a user can drop twenty receipts into an inbox and come back to a drafted report.

Reports are where policy enforcement lives. Administrators define which categories are reimbursable, which require a receipt above a given amount, which need documentation such as mileage logs or client names, and what the per-diem rates are. Rules can warn the submitter, flag a report for a manager or prevent submission outright, and multi-stage approval chains route reports by amount, department or project. Because the checks happen at submission rather than after payment, finance teams spend their time on exceptions.

Reimbursement is handled inside the platform. Approved reports can be paid by ACH transfer to a US bank account, by direct deposit through a connected payroll provider, or through a linked account for employees in other countries. Expensify supports many currencies and applies the exchange rate captured at the time of the expense, which removes the most common source of dispute for internationally distributed teams. Non-US employees without a compatible bank arrangement are typically paid through their local payroll export.

The Expensify Card is a free corporate Visa card offered to companies that use the platform. It integrates directly with the expense workflow, so a card transaction is matched to its receipt automatically and appears on a report that reconciles against the statement without manual work. Card spend earns cash back, and Expensify has historically raised the rate for companies that use SmartScan consistently. Cards can be physical or virtual, assigned per employee with individual limits, and locked or replaced from the dashboard. The card requires a connected business bank account and underwriting on the company's financial position, so eligibility is not automatic.

Accounting integration is mature and broad. Expensify syncs with QuickBooks Online, QuickBooks Desktop, Xero, NetSuite, Sage Intacct and Microsoft Dynamics, exporting coded expenses, receipts and reimbursement journals with a full audit trail of approvals and edits. For companies on an ERP, exports can be shaped through configurable templates.

Expensify Concierge is the company's distinctive support layer, a chat-based assistant available in the app and by email that accepts receipt submissions, answers questions about report status and routes issues to human support. Users can forward a receipt to Concierge without opening the app at all. This design predates the current generation of artificial intelligence features and still shapes how the product feels in daily use.

Beyond expenses, Expensify has grown into a broader finance workflow. Bill pay lets a company pay vendors by card, ACH or check from inside the platform, invoicing covers freelancers and small agencies, and Expensify Travel books flights and hotels with the company policy applied so the expense lands in the report with its itinerary attached. These additions suit a small company that wants one vendor and are largely redundant for a mid-market firm with dedicated procurement and travel tools.

Pricing is per user per month and is organised into paid tiers rather than a free-for-everything model. The entry tier, marketed as Collect, covers unlimited SmartScan receipt capture, expense reports, approval workflows, reimbursement and accounting sync, and is aimed at small teams that need expense reporting without card controls. The higher tier, marketed as Control, adds multi-stage approvals, custom export templates, reimbursement through Expensify's own payment rails in a wider set of countries, the Expensify Card at scale, and domain-level administration. Both tiers cost less when billed annually, and the difference matters at team scale. Free or discounted arrangements have existed for individuals and non-profits, and Expensify runs promotions regularly. Exact current per-seat figures, the annual versus monthly differential and any free allowances should be verified on the Expensify pricing page before committing, because the company has revised its packaging more than once.

Against Ramp and Brex, Expensify is expense-first rather than card-first. Its reimbursement machinery, currency handling and approval routing are deeper, and it works for companies whose employees pay out of pocket and need repaid, which card-centric platforms handle less well, while its controls at the point of authorisation are weaker. Against Dext, Expensify is an end-user expense tool while Dext is aimed at accountants preparing client books. Against SAP Concur, Expensify is considerably cheaper and faster to deploy, with less configurability for complex multinational policy matrices.

The limitations are real. Extraction accuracy degrades on handwritten, damaged or non-Latin-script documents, and users must still correct mistakes. The interface has changed substantially over the years, and the newer application carries a chat-style design that some finance teams find noisy. Advanced configuration, particularly around multi-entity structures and custom export mapping, has a learning curve and sometimes requires support involvement. The Expensify Card is limited by underwriting and by geography, so non-US companies may not be able to use it. Support response times depend on the tier, and heavy reliance on Concierge can frustrate administrators who want a direct escalation path. Per-seat pricing scales linearly with headcount, which becomes expensive for large organisations where only a minority of employees submit expenses.

Expensify fits companies with distributed or travelling employees who pay out of pocket and need reliable reimbursement across borders, accounting practices that want clean coded exports, and small to mid-sized finance teams that prefer a hosted product over configuring an ERP module. It does not fit organisations whose primary need is card-level spend control at authorisation, large enterprises requiring deep policy configurability and on-premises deployment, or businesses with almost no employee spending. When comparing alternatives, Expensify is the strongest choice for reimbursement-heavy workflows with international currency handling, Ramp and Brex are the stronger choices for card-first spend control with free software funded by interchange, and Dext is the right tool when the actual user is an accountant processing client receipts rather than employees submitting their own.

name: Dext
description: Dext Prepare is bookkeeping automation that captures receipts, invoices, and bank data, extracts the fields, and publishes coded transactions to accounting packages. Widely used by accounting firms processing client bookkeeping at volume.
overview:
Dext is a bookkeeping automation platform whose primary user is an accountant or bookkeeper rather than the business owner. It began life in the United Kingdom as Receipt Bank, rebranded to Dext, and split its offering into named products that map to stages of the accounting workflow: Dext Prepare for capturing and extracting purchase and sales documents, Dext Extract for pulling bank and card feed data, Dext Precision for reconciliation and VAT or sales tax return preparation, and Dext Commerce for bringing e-commerce platform data into the books. The company is headquartered in Essex and has strong adoption among UK, Irish, Australian, New Zealand, Canadian, South African and United States practices. An accountancy firm processing documents for fifty or five hundred clients is the archetype customer, and the product is designed around that scale.

Dext Prepare is the product most people mean when they say Dext. Documents enter the system through several routes: the mobile app, where a user photographs a receipt or invoice, an email-in function that gives each client a unique address so suppliers and staff can forward documents directly, a desktop bulk uploader that accepts folders of images and PDFs, and integrations that pull documents from cloud storage. Once a document is in, extraction reads it and identifies the supplier, the date, the net amount, the tax amount, the total and the currency. Dext claims very high extraction accuracy on standard printed supplier invoices and receipts, and the practical exceptions are handwritten documents, unusual international formats, multi-page invoices where the totals sit on a later page, and heavily stylised point-of-sale printouts.

What makes the extraction useful rather than merely impressive is the rules engine. An accountant can define supplier-level rules so that a document from a known utility provider always codes to a specific nominal account, always applies a specific tax treatment and always lands in the right client's ledger. Rules can also match on document type, amount range and currency. Because the same suppliers recur month after month, the proportion of documents needing human attention falls steadily after the first few weeks, and the work shifts from data entry to review.

Publication to accounting software is the other half of the workflow. Dext Prepare publishes extracted transactions to Xero, QuickBooks Online, QuickBooks Desktop, Sage Business Cloud Accounting, Sage 50, FreeAgent and other systems, with the original document image attached to the resulting transaction. That attachment matters for compliance, because it means the source document travels with the ledger entry and is available during a tax enquiry or an audit without anyone going back to a shoebox or a shared drive. Dext stores documents for a defined retention period, which is long enough to cover statutory record-keeping requirements in its main markets, and the retention length and the legal basis for it should be confirmed against the current service terms for the relevant jurisdiction.

Dext Extract addresses the bank side, connecting to bank and card feeds through open banking and aggregation partners and normalising the transaction data into the same working environment as the captured documents. Dext Precision builds on that with reconciliation tooling and tax return preparation, moving a practice from extracted data to a completed periodic return with an audit trail of what was reviewed and by whom.

Dext Commerce is aimed at e-commerce clients, which are notoriously painful to bookkeep because a single settlement from a marketplace bundles hundreds of individual orders, fees, refunds and shipping charges. Dext Commerce ingests data from platforms such as Shopify and from payment processors such as Stripe and PayPal, breaks settlements into their components and publishes coherent journal entries. For a practice with a meaningful number of online sellers, this product alone can justify the subscription.

Practice management features are built for the multi-client reality. An accountant works across a portfolio from one dashboard, sees document volume and processing status per client, assigns work to team members and controls permissions. Client-facing access lets a business owner upload documents into their own space without seeing anything belonging to another client, which is a basic requirement for any firm handling competing businesses.

Pricing is structured around the accounting practice rather than around individual users, and it is the area that most needs verification before purchase. Dext Prepare for accountants is typically sold per client per month, with volume tiers so that the per-client price falls as the number of clients grows, and with document volume or feature boundaries between tiers. There are also packages that bundle Prepare with Extract, Precision and Commerce, and separate pricing for businesses buying Dext directly rather than through their accountant, which is available in some markets and not others. Pricing differs by region, and Dext has revised its packaging several times, so current per-client costs, tier thresholds and bundle contents should be confirmed on the Dext pricing page or with its sales team.

Against Expensify, Dext serves a different user. Expensify is bought by a company so its own employees can submit expense reports and get reimbursed, while Dext is bought by an accountant so that documents from many companies can be extracted, coded and published into ledgers. The two overlap on receipt capture and are frequently used together. Against Hubdoc, which Xero owns and includes with some Xero subscriptions, Dext offers deeper rules, better multi-client practice management and a broader product range, at a price a firm must justify against a tool that may already be bundled. Against doing the work manually, the comparison is straightforward: an hour of keying invoices costs more than the subscription for almost any practice above a handful of clients.

The limitations deserve attention. Dext is not an accounting system, so it must be paired with Xero, QuickBooks, Sage or another ledger, and its value depends on that pairing being clean. Extraction quality degrades on handwritten, damaged, multi-page and non-standard documents, and a practice still needs a review step. Rules require initial configuration effort, and a poorly designed rule set produces confidently wrong coding that is slower to fix than manual entry. Bank feed reliability depends on the underlying aggregation partners, and the interface is functional rather than polished, so new staff need training. Regional availability varies, particularly for the direct-to-business packages.

Dext fits accountancy practices and bookkeeping firms processing documents for multiple clients, especially those with e-commerce or high supplier-invoice volume, and in-house finance teams that receive a large number of purchase invoices each month and want them coded and published to the ledger automatically. It does not fit sole traders with a handful of receipts a month, companies whose main problem is employee reimbursement and travel policy, or organisations that need an all-in-one accounting system rather than a capture and extraction layer. When comparing alternatives, Dext is the strongest choice for accountant-led, multi-client bookkeeping automation with publication into Xero, QuickBooks or Sage, Hubdoc is the value option for firms already paying for Xero, Expensify is the right tool for employee expense reporting and reimbursement, and a dedicated accounts payable platform is a better fit when the requirement is approval workflows and vendor payments rather than document extraction.

name: Chargebee
description: Chargebee is a subscription billing platform handling recurring invoicing, proration, plan changes, tax calculation, dunning, and revenue recognition. Offers hosted checkout pages, a broad integration catalog, and reporting for SaaS and subscription businesses.
overview:
Chargebee is a subscription billing and revenue management platform for software-as-a-service companies, membership and content businesses, subscription boxes and B2B firms with recurring invoicing. It was founded in 2011 in Chennai, India, and has grown into one of the larger independent players in a category that also includes Recurly, Zuora and the billing modules inside payment processors. The problem it solves is narrow but deep. Once a business has more than a handful of plans, more than one payment method, tax obligations in multiple jurisdictions and customers who upgrade, downgrade, pause and cancel at will, a hand-built billing system on top of a payment gateway becomes the most fragile part of the stack. Chargebee replaces it with a configurable billing engine and a set of hosted pages.

The billing engine handles the subscription lifecycle. Plans are defined with a billing period, a price, a currency and included quantities, add-ons attach with their own pricing, and coupons apply percentage or fixed discounts for a defined period. Trials, introductory pricing and setup fees are configuration rather than code. When a customer upgrades mid-cycle, Chargebee calculates proration, credits the unused portion of the old plan, charges the difference and starts the new entitlement immediately, and downgrades, pauses and cancellations follow the same logic. This proration machinery is the hardest part of subscription billing to build correctly and the main reason companies adopt a platform.

Hosted checkout and a self-service customer portal remove the need to build payment collection and account management interfaces. The checkout page can be embedded in a site or opened as a redirect, supports card, direct debit, wallet and local payment methods, and is maintained by Chargebee so that changes in card network rules do not require a release from the customer's engineering team. The portal lets subscribers view invoices, update payment details, change plans and cancel without contacting support.

Payment coverage is broad and gateway-agnostic. Chargebee connects to a large number of gateways and processors, including Stripe, Adyen, Braintree, Checkout.com, Authorize.net, PayPal and GoCardless, and supports many currencies. A company can route different regions or business units to different gateways from one configuration and can switch gateway without rebuilding billing logic. Because Chargebee sits above the processor rather than replacing it, payment fees continue to be paid to the underlying gateway.

Dunning and receivable recovery address involuntary churn, which is typically a larger revenue leak than voluntary cancellation. When a payment fails, Chargebee retries on a configurable schedule, sends email notifications at each stage, offers a page where the customer can update the card, and moves the subscription to a past-due, suspended or cancelled state according to rules. Smart dunning adapts retry timing to the decline reason, and card account updater services refresh reissued card numbers.

Tax and compliance are handled through integrations rather than a bundled engine. Chargebee connects to Avalara, Vertex, TaxJar and Stripe Tax, calculates the correct tax per jurisdiction and records it on the invoice, and it supports the invoice numbering and disclosure requirements that differ between the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, India and Australia.

Revenue accounting is where Chargebee moves beyond billing into the finance function. It calculates deferred revenue, produces recognition schedules aligned to ASC 606 and IFRS 15, generates MRR and cohort churn reports, and exports journals to NetSuite, QuickBooks, Xero and Sage Intacct. For a company preparing for fundraising or an audit, a defensible recognition trail that reconciles to the general ledger is often the decisive requirement.

B2B capabilities extend the platform beyond self-serve subscriptions. Chargebee supports quotes and CPQ-style workflows with custom pricing and discounts, contract terms with committed amounts and overage, purchase order capture, invoicing on milestones or in arrears, and collections for unpaid invoices. Its managed receivables product handles B2B invoicing and reminders for companies whose revenue is recurring but not card-based.

Integration and extensibility round out the platform. Chargebee publishes a REST API, webhooks for every lifecycle event, client libraries in several languages, and native connectors to Salesforce, HubSpot, NetSuite, QuickBooks, Xero and analytics warehouses, so a company can treat Chargebee as the system of record for entitlements.

Security posture matters because the platform touches payment data. Chargebee operates as a PCI DSS Level 1 service provider and maintains SOC report coverage, and hosted pages keep card details away from the merchant's own servers, reducing the merchant's PCI scope. The specific current attestations and report types should be confirmed with Chargebee during procurement, since certification status is re-issued annually.

Pricing follows a usage-based structure with a free entry tier. The Starter plan has historically been free until cumulative billed revenue crosses a defined threshold, which is on the order of a few hundred thousand dollars. Above that sits the Performance plan, which carries a monthly platform fee, includes an allowance of billing volume and charges a percentage overage above it. Enterprise pricing is negotiated and adds higher volume allowances, dedicated support and advanced modules. Chargebee has repackaged its plans more than once, and the monthly fee, the volume thresholds and the overage percentage have all moved, so current figures must be checked on its pricing page or in a quote rather than assumed from older material. The overage percentage is the number to model carefully, because at high billing volume it dominates total cost.

Against Stripe Billing, Chargebee offers deeper subscription configuration, better revenue recognition and multi-gateway flexibility, while Stripe Billing is cheaper and simpler for a company that only needs Stripe. Against Recurly the two are close competitors, and the choice comes down to references and pricing model. Against Zuora, Chargebee is easier to implement and far cheaper. Against building in-house, Chargebee costs money but removes months of engineering work, and the in-house route almost always underestimates tax, proration and dunning complexity.

The limitations are worth naming. Percentage-based overage makes costs rise with success, so a fast-growing company can see its billing expense grow faster than headcount. Some advanced modules and the deepest revenue accounting features are gated to higher tiers. Configuration breadth creates a learning curve, and a poorly modelled plan structure is expensive to unwind once customers are attached to it. Support responsiveness varies by tier. Chargebee does not replace a payment gateway, so gateway fees remain, and it lacks the fraud tooling and dispute management depth of a dedicated processor.

Chargebee fits subscription businesses between roughly the first paying customer and mid-market scale, particularly SaaS companies selling in multiple currencies and jurisdictions, B2B firms with quoted contracts and invoicing, and any company that needs defensible revenue recognition without an ERP implementation. It does not fit very simple single-plan businesses that would be better served by Stripe Billing or a gateway's native subscriptions, one-off payment businesses with no recurrence, and large enterprises whose rating complexity genuinely requires Zuora. When comparing alternatives, Chargebee is the strongest all-round choice for configurable subscription billing plus revenue management at a mid-market price, Stripe Billing wins on simplicity and cost for Stripe-only companies, Recurly competes closely on the same ground with different enterprise references, and Zuora is the right answer only when scale and rating complexity justify the implementation cost.

name: Paddle
description: Paddle is a merchant of record for software companies, taking legal ownership of each sale so it handles payment processing, sales tax and VAT registration, invoicing, chargebacks, and compliance. Suits SaaS and digital product sellers that want to avoid registering for tax in every market.
overview:
Paddle is a billing and revenue platform built specifically for software companies that sell to customers around the world. What separates it from most payment tools is the commercial structure underneath it. Paddle operates as a merchant of record, which means that when a customer buys a subscription or a licence, the legal seller on the transaction is Paddle rather than the software vendor. Paddle collects the money, keeps its fee, and remits the balance to the company on a regular payout schedule. Founded in London in 2012, it serves business-to-business and business-to-consumer software products, from single-developer utilities to established SaaS businesses generating millions in annual recurring revenue.

The merchant of record model is the core value proposition, and it is worth being precise about what it changes. When you use a payment service provider such as Stripe, Square or PayPal, you remain the merchant. You hold the customer relationship, you are liable for chargebacks, and you are responsible for registering with tax authorities, calculating the right tax at checkout, filing returns, and remitting money in every jurisdiction where you have a taxable presence. When you use Paddle, those obligations transfer to Paddle itself. It registers for value added tax, goods and services tax and US sales tax where required, computes the correct amount per transaction, files the returns, and pays the authorities. It also absorbs chargeback disputes, runs fraud screening, and produces invoices that satisfy local documentation rules for software sales.

That shift matters most for small teams selling internationally. Since the 2018 South Dakota v. Wayfair decision, a software company can owe US sales tax in states where it has no physical presence once it crosses economic thresholds. In the European Union, digital services sold to consumers are taxed where the buyer sits, and the One Stop Shop scheme still requires registration, quarterly filings and record keeping. For a company with two employees, doing this correctly across dozens of countries can cost more than the software itself. Paddle removes the need to build or buy that capability, which is why it is most often chosen by SaaS businesses that have outgrown a simple checkout but do not yet have a finance function.

On billing, Paddle provides the full subscription engine rather than just a payment form. It handles recurring charges, trial conversions, prorated upgrades and downgrades, seat changes, add-ons, coupons, multi-year terms and mixed one-off plus recurring charges on a single invoice. Failed payments are retried on a schedule built around card network rules, with customer-facing update flows that recover revenue which would otherwise churn. Because Paddle is the seller, the invoice comes from Paddle, and the company's records reflect a single settlement entry rather than thousands of individual consumer transactions.

The checkout layer supports a hosted page, an embedded overlay and React or JavaScript components for teams that want tighter control of their own UI. Customers can pay by card, by regional payment methods and bank transfer schemes depending on their country, and by digital wallets. Prices can be localized so a customer in Germany sees euros inclusive of tax while a US customer sees dollars with tax added at checkout. Payment links let a company bill without building a page at all.

Retention tooling rounds out the product. Paddle Retain, which grew out of the Churnkey acquisition, adds cancellation flows, save offers, pause options and churn analytics so a business can intervene before a subscription ends. Around that sit revenue dashboards, subscription analytics, alerts, reporting exports, a sandbox, a documented REST API and webhooks for lifecycle events.

The difference from a payment service provider is therefore structural rather than feature-by-feature. Stripe gives you infrastructure and leaves compliance with you. Stripe Tax will calculate tax and Stripe Billing will manage subscriptions, but your company still registers in each jurisdiction, files returns, carries chargeback liability, and pays separately for the tax engine. Paddle bundles all of that into one fee and takes on the legal exposure. Comparable merchant of record offerings include FastSpring, Lemon Squeezy, which Stripe acquired in 2024, Gumroad for creator and digital-download sales, and Polar for open-source and developer products. Against those, Paddle is generally positioned as the enterprise-capable option with deeper subscription logic and a longer compliance track record.

Pricing is a single blended rate rather than a stack of separate fees. Paddle's published standard pricing is 5 percent plus 50 cents per completed transaction, with no monthly subscription, no setup fee and no separate charge for tax filing or chargeback handling. That figure should be confirmed on Paddle's pricing page before you model it, because the company has adjusted its terms over time and negotiated rates are available at higher volumes. On a 20 dollar subscription the fee is 1.50 dollars, or 7.5 percent, while on a 500 dollar annual invoice it is 25.50 dollars, or about 5.1 percent. Compared with a payment service provider at roughly 2.9 percent plus 30 cents the premium is real, and it is offset by what you no longer pay for: tax registration services, compliance software, filing software, accounting hours and dispute management.

The limitations follow from the same structure. Paddle only handles software, digital products and services, so physical goods, professional services delivered offline and most marketplace models fall outside its scope. Onboarding involves an approval process with restricted categories and a review of what you sell, and not every applicant is accepted. Payouts run on a fixed schedule with a reserve held back to cover refunds and chargebacks, which affects cash flow compared with next-day settlement. Customers also transact with Paddle, so branding on receipts and ownership of payment data sit differently than they would with your own merchant account. You cannot bring your own acquiring bank or negotiated interchange rates, and at high volumes the 5 percent headline rate becomes materially more expensive than running a payment service provider plus a tax engine.

Paddle fits small and mid-sized software companies selling internationally without a finance team, developer-tool vendors, SaaS founders who want tax handled rather than managed, and businesses whose customer base is spread across enough countries that self-managing compliance is genuinely expensive. It is a poor fit for businesses selling physical inventory, marketplaces that onboard their own sellers, companies in restricted verticals, very high-volume businesses where a two percentage point difference is a large sum, and organizations that already run a mature tax function.

Against the alternatives, the choice reduces to who should own compliance. If you want maximum control, the broadest set of payment methods and the lowest marginal cost, a payment service provider plus a tax calculation product usually wins on economics once you have internal finance capacity. If you want one vendor to be the seller of record so tax registration, filing, remittance, invoicing and disputes stop being your problem, Paddle is one of the most established ways to buy that outcome, and for a small team selling globally the fee is often cheaper than the compliance work it replaces.

name: PayPal
description: PayPal operates a global consumer wallet alongside merchant services including online checkout buttons, invoicing, card processing through Braintree, point-of-sale hardware, and working capital. Buyers pay from a balance, bank account, card, or PayPal Credit.
overview:
PayPal is a payments company that operates on two sides of the same transaction. To consumers it is a digital wallet holding balances, linked bank accounts and cards, used to pay online and to send money to other people. To merchants it is a payment processor, a checkout button with enormous brand recognition, and a set of tools for invoicing, in-person selling and cross-border transfers. The company traces back to 1998, was owned by eBay from 2002 to 2015, and has been an independent listed business since the spin-off. It reports hundreds of millions of active accounts worldwide, and that installed base is the reason merchants keep using it even when cheaper processors exist.

The consumer side matters to a business because it changes what happens at checkout. A buyer who has a PayPal account can complete a purchase without typing a card number or an address, because PayPal supplies the funding source and the shipping details. That reduces form friction and abandonment on mobile in particular. Venmo, acquired along with Braintree in 2013, adds a second consumer brand with a strong following among younger American buyers. Pay Later and instalment options let customers split a purchase at PayPal's cost rather than the merchant's. Buyer Protection, which gives purchasers roughly 180 days to open a dispute and potentially receive a refund, is a genuine conversion asset for unknown retailers and a genuine risk for merchants selling goods that are easy to dispute.

For merchants, the current core product is PayPal Complete Payments, a single platform that consolidates what used to be several separate integrations. It offers the familiar PayPal and Venmo buttons, a standard card checkout that redirects or opens a modal, and an advanced card option that lets you render your own card fields while PayPal keeps the card data off your servers. Alongside it sit invoicing with hosted payment pages, payment links and QR codes that need no website at all, a virtual terminal for card payments taken over the phone, subscription and recurring billing, and PayPal Zettle, the point-of-sale system with card readers for physical shops. Business accounts also get a debit card and, in some markets, a PayPal Balance that can hold and earn on funds.

Braintree is the developer-facing brand inside the same company and remains separate from the standard merchant experience. It processes cards directly alongside PayPal, Venmo, Apple Pay and Google Pay through one integration, offers a Drop-in UI that renders all of those methods with a single block of code, and supports recurring billing and marketplace-style payments. Braintree is what a platform chooses when it wants PayPal as one method among many rather than as the primary identity of its checkout.

Cross-border capability is one of PayPal's older strengths. The network supports receiving payments in a large number of currencies and settling in a smaller set of local currencies, which lets a freelancer or an online shop sell internationally without opening foreign bank accounts. Xoom, acquired in 2015, handles consumer remittance and transfers to bank accounts, cash pickup locations and mobile wallets. The commercial catch is conversion. PayPal converts at its own rate rather than the mid-market rate, and the spread plus any fixed fee is where a meaningful part of the true cost of an international transaction sits.

PayPal has also expanded into financial services. Working Capital and Business Loan products advance money against future sales, repaid from a percentage of daily revenue, and savings products for business balances have been offered through partner banks in the United States.

Compared with its competitors, PayPal is wallet-led rather than API-led. Stripe offers more products, more payment methods and more consistent documentation, but it does not arrive with a consumer account base that customers already trust and already have funded. Square is built around hardware and vertical software for physical small businesses, an area where Zettle competes with less depth. Adyen, Checkout.com and Braintree's own enterprise offering compete on a single global acquiring platform and negotiated interchange-plus pricing at high volume. Paddle and similar merchants of record take on tax and compliance liability, which PayPal does not do for a standard merchant account. PayPal's distinct position is that it is simultaneously a payment method and a processor, and the payment method part carries consumer trust that a gateway cannot manufacture.

Pricing is transaction-based for the standard business account, with no monthly fee to open or maintain it in most markets. The structure has several rates rather than one. Transactions funded from a customer's PayPal balance or a linked Venmo account carry one rate, online card transactions through PayPal Complete Payments carry a lower rate, advanced card integrations may carry a different rate again, and Zettle in-person transactions have their own published card-present rate. Each is a percentage plus a fixed per-transaction fee, and the fixed fee varies by currency. Braintree publishes a separate standard card rate, historically around 2.59 percent plus 49 cents for US online transactions, with PayPal and Venmo transactions priced higher. Chargebacks incur a fixed dispute fee, and international transactions add cross-border and conversion charges. PayPal has changed merchant pricing several times and rates differ substantially by country, so current figures should be confirmed on its pricing page rather than assumed.

The limitations are well documented by merchants. Account limitation and reserve practices are the most serious concern. PayPal's risk systems can hold funds, impose a rolling reserve for up to 180 days, or close an account with limited warning, and its Acceptable Use Policy is enforced broadly. Appeals are slow, which for a business whose only processor is PayPal becomes an existential risk rather than an inconvenience. Disputes tend to resolve in favour of the buyer under Buyer Protection, particularly for goods that are hard to prove delivered. The fee schedule is complex and varies by region, checkout customization is more constrained than with an API-first provider, and the PayPal and Braintree dashboards and support channels remain distinct.

PayPal fits businesses that sell to consumers who already have accounts, marketplaces that want Venmo and wallet payments without building several integrations, freelancers invoicing internationally without any code, and shops that want a recognized brand on the checkout page to reduce buyer hesitation. It is a poor sole choice for high-volume businesses that can negotiate better rates, for sellers in categories the Acceptable Use Policy treats restrictively, for companies that cannot tolerate a processor-initiated hold on cash, and for engineering teams that need deep control over the payment flow.

The practical pattern among mature businesses is not to choose one. Most run an API-first processor as the primary rail and offer PayPal as an additional method, because it converts customers who would otherwise abandon and because keeping volume elsewhere limits the damage of an account hold. Evaluated on its own terms, PayPal is the strongest consumer-trust payment method available and a capable but less predictable merchant platform.

name: Stripe
description: Stripe is a payments platform providing APIs for accepting card and wallet payments, subscription billing, marketplace payouts through Connect, in-person payments with Terminal, fraud screening with Radar, and financial infrastructure such as issuing and Treasury.
overview:
Stripe is a payments and financial infrastructure company that sells its capability primarily through APIs. Founded in 2010 by Patrick and John Collison and headquartered in South San Francisco with a large operation in Dublin, it became the reference implementation for developer-led commerce. Its customers range from individual developers charging their first subscription to public companies processing billions of dollars in annual volume. The defining characteristic of Stripe is that almost everything it offers, from a single card charge to a global marketplace payout, is exposed as a documented, versioned interface that an engineer can integrate in an afternoon and scale for years.

At the centre sits the core payments API. Payment Intents model the lifecycle of a transaction, separating authorization from confirmation and capturing the state transitions that card networks and regional schemes actually require. On top of that, Stripe Checkout provides a hosted payment page and Payment Element an embeddable component, both handling card entry, digital wallets such as Apple Pay and Google Pay, and Stripe's own Link wallet. The platform supports more than 135 currencies and dozens of local payment methods, including SEPA direct debit, ACH, iDEAL, Bancontact, Klarna and Afterpay-style instalments, Alipay, WeChat Pay and Boleto, with availability varying by country. Adaptive acceptance and network-level retry logic lift authorization rates.

Stripe Billing turns those primitives into a subscription and invoicing system. It supports recurring billing on any schedule, tiered and volume pricing, per-seat quantity changes, usage-based and metered charges fed from events, prorated upgrades and downgrades, trials, coupons, multi-currency price books, and hosted invoice pages with reminders. Revenue recovery handles failed payments through smart retries and customer-facing card update flows. Billing is priced as a percentage of billing volume on top of the underlying processing fee.

Connect is the product for platforms and marketplaces. It lets a business onboard other businesses or individuals as sellers, choose between Standard, Express and Custom account types depending on how much of the flow it wants to own, split payments between the platform and its sellers at charge time, schedule payouts, and handle identity verification and the tax reporting that payouts to third parties require. Connect is why a large share of US marketplaces run on Stripe, and it is a hard capability to reproduce with a plain gateway.

Risk tooling sits alongside. Radar applies machine learning trained on transaction data flowing across the whole Stripe network, which gives it a data advantage over a fraud product used by a single merchant. Rules block, review or allow payments based on attributes, Three-D Secure and Strong Customer Authentication are handled in the integration layer, and a dispute workflow manages chargeback evidence.

Beyond payments, Stripe has assembled a wider financial stack. Terminal provides in-person acceptance with certified readers and the same API surface as online payments. Atlas incorporates a company in Delaware with a tax identification number and bank account for a fixed fee. Issuing creates physical or virtual cards, Treasury offers banking primitives for platforms, Capital lends against future card volume, Identity verifies documents, Financial Connections reads bank data, Tax calculates rates where you are registered, Sigma and Data Pipeline give SQL access to Stripe data, and Climate allocates revenue to carbon removal.

The developer experience is the practical reason teams choose Stripe. There are official libraries for the major languages, a command-line tool for local webhook testing, test mode with simulated failure states, sandboxes for isolated environments, and documentation with runnable examples. Webhooks, idempotency keys and predictable error objects make the integration testable.

Compared with its rivals, Stripe is infrastructure rather than a wallet or a point-of-sale vendor. PayPal leads with a consumer brand and hundreds of millions of funded accounts, which lifts conversion for buyers who already have a balance, but its merchant tooling has historically been assembled from separate acquisitions. Square leads with hardware and vertical software for physical small businesses and publishes flat rates that need no negotiation. Adyen, Checkout.com and Braintree compete on a single global acquiring platform and interchange-plus pricing that becomes cheaper at very high volume. Paddle and FastSpring are merchants of record that take on tax and compliance liability, which Stripe does not do.

Pricing in the United States is published and volume-based rather than contract-based for most accounts. Online card charges cost 2.9 percent plus 30 cents per successful transaction. In-person payments through Terminal or Tap to Pay cost 2.7 percent plus 5 cents. International cards add around 1.5 percent, and currency conversion adds a further percentage when Stripe converts the funds. Manually keyed card numbers cost more than card-present transactions. There is no monthly fee and no setup fee for the standard account. Billing is charged as a percentage of billing volume, with a lower rate on the Starter tier and a higher rate on Scale, commonly quoted at 0.5 and 0.8 percent respectively. Radar for Fraud Teams adds a per-screened-payment fee on top of the included protection, Stripe Tax charges per calculated transaction, and instant payouts to a debit card cost around 1.75 percent of the amount moved. These figures change and vary by country, so current numbers should be confirmed on Stripe's pricing page before building a financial model.

The limitations are worth naming. You remain the merchant of record, so sales tax registration, filing and remittance stay with you even if Stripe Tax does the calculation. Account risk management is automated and can produce sudden holds, reserves or terminations that are difficult to appeal, which is a genuine business-continuity risk for companies dependent on a single processor. Support for smaller accounts is limited compared with the dedicated engineering support larger accounts receive. The product range is wide enough that teams often pay for overlapping products, and consolidating reporting across them takes work. Published rates are not negotiable until volume is significant, so interchange-plus pricing only becomes available through a custom agreement. Terminal's hardware ecosystem is narrower than Square's, and Stripe is not a natural choice for a business that mostly sells in person.

Stripe fits software companies, marketplaces, subscription businesses and any team that wants programmatic control over payments and expects to grow into more of the platform. It is a weaker fit for a sole trader who needs a card reader and simple invoicing today, for businesses whose model requires the processor to own tax liability, and for very high-volume enterprises that can negotiate materially better terms elsewhere.

Against the alternatives, the decision is usually about where the complexity lives. Square is easier if your business is physical, PayPal is stronger if consumer wallet trust drives conversion, and a merchant of record is better if compliance is the bottleneck. For anything built as software, Stripe's API surface, documentation and product breadth remain the benchmark.

name: Square
description: Square from Block provides point-of-sale software and hardware, online checkout, invoicing, payment processing, payroll, team management, loans, and banking products for small and mid-sized businesses, all under one account across online and in-person sales.
overview:
Square is the small business arm of Block, Inc., the company founded in 2009 by Jack Dorsey and Jim McKelvey and renamed from Square, Inc. in 2021. Block now also owns Cash App and TIDAL, but Square remains the brand aimed at merchants. Its original product was a small card reader that plugged into a phone headphone jack and let anyone accept card payments, which changed the economics of selling in person. Today it is a full commerce platform covering point-of-sale software, payment processing, hardware, websites, invoicing, payroll, banking products and business loans, sold to retail shops, restaurants, appointment-based services, professional firms, nonprofits and online sellers.

The point-of-sale software is the anchor and it is free. The Square Point of Sale app runs on iOS, Android and in a browser, and it handles the item catalogue, variants and modifiers, inventory counts, discounts, tips, split tenders, refunds, exchanges, receipts by email or text, employee permissions and time tracking, and sales reporting. Because the same app serves a food truck, a boutique and a salon, Square builds vertical versions on top of it rather than separate products. Square for Retail adds vendor management, purchase orders, barcode labels and cost of goods reporting. Square for Restaurants adds course and seat management, table layout, kitchen display screens and bar tab handling. Square Appointments adds service lists, staff calendars, booking pages, deposit collection and no-show handling.

Hardware is designed to work with that software out of the box and is sold outright rather than leased. The lineup runs from a contactless and chip reader through Square Handheld, Square Stand, Square Terminal as a self-contained wireless device with a built-in printer, and Square Register with a customer-facing display. All accept tap, dip and swipe, support digital wallets, and run on a single merchant account, so adding a second location needs no new contract. Tap to Pay accepts contactless payments on a supported iPhone or Android phone with no external device, removing the hardware cost barrier for very small sellers.

Payment acceptance extends well beyond the card reader. Square Invoices sends invoices with online payment links, supports deposits, recurring billing and late-payment reminders, and charges no fee beyond the transaction cost. Square Online is a store builder that shares the item catalogue with the point-of-sale system, so inventory stays synchronized across channels, and supports local pickup, delivery, shipping and restaurant ordering pages. Virtual terminal covers card-not-present payments taken by phone. Gift cards, loyalty programs, email and text marketing campaigns, and customer directories with purchase histories are all first-party features. Installment payments come through Afterpay, acquired by Block in 2022, and Cash App Pay gives access to the Cash App consumer base.

The financial services layer is where Square has grown most. Square Banking bundles business checking with no monthly fee, interest-bearing savings, instant transfer of same-day settlement to a debit card for a fee, and predictable release schedules. Square Loans advances working capital based on a business's own card processing history, repaid as a fixed percentage of daily sales rather than through a monthly instalment. Square Payroll runs pay cycles, files state and federal taxes, handles direct deposit and contractor payments, and integrates with benefits providers in the United States.

Reporting and integration round out the platform. The dashboard consolidates sales across locations and channels, tracks item-level performance, supports employee labour reporting and exports to accounting packages including QuickBooks Online and Xero. Square's developer platform exposes APIs for payments, orders, catalog, customers, inventory, employees, loyalty and subscriptions with webhooks, which lets a business build custom flows on top of Square rather than replacing it.

Compared with its competitors, Square is turnkey where others are components. Stripe is infrastructure for engineers, offering a broader API surface, more payment methods and more flexibility, but it does not ship a register, a restaurant menu system or a payroll product. Shopify leads with e-commerce and treats in-person selling as an extension of its storefront, so it suits businesses where online is the primary channel. Toast competes directly in restaurants with proprietary hardware and is generally deeper on kitchen operations, at higher cost and with longer contracts. Clover sells through banks and resellers with variable pricing, Lightspeed goes deeper for complex multistore retail, and PayPal Zettle covers similar ground in some markets with less software around it. Square's advantage is that one vendor, one account, one dashboard and one published price list covers the register, the website, the invoices and the payroll.

Pricing is published and flat, with no monthly fee for the core offering. In-person tap, dip and swipe transactions in the United States cost 2.6 percent plus 10 cents. Online card-not-present transactions cost 2.9 percent plus 30 cents. Manually keyed payments and card invoices carry a higher rate, around 3.5 percent plus 15 cents, reflecting the greater fraud risk of a number typed by hand. There are no long-term contracts, no early termination fee and no PCI compliance fee, and hardware is a one-time purchase. The paid software tiers for Retail, Restaurants, Appointments and Online add a per-location monthly subscription on top of the same processing rates, and Payroll adds a monthly base fee plus a per-employee charge. These are US figures and change periodically, so the rates for your market should be confirmed on Square's pricing page.

The limitations are the mirror of the advantages. Flat published pricing means there is little room to negotiate, so a business doing several million dollars in card volume pays close to the same rate as a market stall, whereas an interchange-plus agreement with another processor could be cheaper. Vertical software is broad but not always as deep as a specialist, and complex retailers, multi-location restaurant groups and manufacturers often outgrow it. The platform is available in a limited set of countries, including the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia, Japan, France and Spain, so it is not an option for merchants elsewhere. Account risk decisions and fund holds do occur, though less commonly reported than with wallet-based processors, and support is largely self-service and chat based for smaller merchants. Add-on costs accumulate quickly once payroll, loyalty, marketing, premium reporting and paid software tiers are all switched on.

Square fits businesses that sell in person, or in person and online together, and want to be operational in a day without an engineering team. It is the strongest default for a new retail shop, a food business, a salon, a tradesperson invoicing customers, or a market seller who needs a reader and a free app. It is a weaker choice for a software company selling subscriptions internationally, for businesses that need custom payment flows, for very high-volume merchants who can negotiate better rates, and for merchants in countries Square does not serve.

Against the alternatives, Square trades flexibility for completeness. Stripe gives more control and a lower cost at scale if you can build, Shopify is better if the website is the business, and Toast and Lightspeed go deeper in their verticals. Square is the choice when the priority is a working system today, from one vendor, at prices published on a single page.

name: Wave
description: Wave is accounting software for freelancers and micro businesses offering free bookkeeping, invoicing, and receipt scanning, with paid payment processing, payroll, and advisor services. Runs in the browser with no seat charge for the core accounting product.
overview:
Wave is accounting software that gives away the accounting and charges for the money movement around it. Built by Wave Financial Inc., founded in Toronto in 2010 and acquired by H&R Block in 2019, it targets the smallest end of the business spectrum. Freelancers, consultants, independent contractors, sole proprietors, micro agencies and small service businesses use it to keep a proper set of books, send invoices and stay organized for tax season without paying a software subscription. The commercial logic is that a business with one or two people does not want to pay for accounting software, and that if the software is free it becomes the natural place to process card payments, run payroll and buy bookkeeping help, which is what Wave charges for.

The accounting core is genuine double-entry bookkeeping rather than a simple income and expense tracker. Every transaction posts to a chart of accounts, which can use a standard template or a customized set, and the ledger produces a balance sheet, an income statement, a statement of cash flow and a general ledger report. Bank and card accounts connect to import transactions automatically, and those transactions can be matched against invoices and bills or categorized with rules that learn from repeated patterns. Reconciliation confirms the ledger against a bank statement, the step an accountant expects to be done before filing a return. Multi-currency is supported with automatic exchange rate handling, so a freelancer billing a client in euros can keep books in dollars.

Invoicing is the feature most users arrive for. Wave offers customizable invoice templates with a logo and brand colors, estimates that convert into invoices, recurring invoices on any schedule, deposits and partial payments, automatic payment reminders to chase overdue invoices, and the ability to accept payment directly from the invoice through a card or bank transfer. Invoices and estimates are unlimited on the free plan, which is the point of differentiation against tools that cap the free tier by document count or revenue. Payment links allow a business to collect money without a website, and receipts can be issued alongside invoices.

Expense handling covers the other half of the ledger. Bank imports capture spending automatically, the mobile app photographs receipts and attaches them to transactions, and expenses are categorized for deduction purposes at tax time. Employee and contractor reimbursement can be tracked, and in some markets Wave has offered business banking features and a payment card tied to the account so spending flows into the books directly. Availability varies by country, so it should be checked against what is currently offered.

Payroll is a paid product and one of the two main revenue sources. In the United States it runs pay cycles, calculates and files federal and state payroll taxes, supports direct deposit, handles year-end tax forms, and offers full-service filing in all fifty states with self-service options in a smaller number. Canadian payroll is available in parallel. Payroll is priced as a monthly base fee plus a per-employee charge, and the figures depend on service level and state, so current pricing should be confirmed on Wave's site.

Wave Advisors is the human-services layer. Instead of only selling software, Wave sells done-for-you bookkeeping, accounting coaching sessions and sales tax filing help, all delivered by Wave staff working inside the same account. That suits an owner who would rather pay someone to close the books than learn the software, and it keeps the relationship inside one vendor. These are subscription or session-based services with their own published pricing.

Compared with its competitors, Wave's position is unusual. QuickBooks Online is the default in the United States with the largest accountant ecosystem and the deepest feature set, but every meaningful tier costs money and prices have risen repeatedly. Xero is cloud-native and strong in the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand with solid multi-user controls, but it has no genuine free plan. Zoho Books offers a free tier capped by annual revenue and grows into a full suite of business apps, making it the closest structural rival. FreshBooks is invoicing-led and prices per user. Sage has a long history in the United Kingdom and mid-market products above the small business tier. Wave is the only one of these where the accounting software itself costs nothing indefinitely and does not cap invoices or transactions by revenue.

Pricing is therefore split. The software is free with unlimited invoices, unlimited receipts, unlimited transactions and the ability to add collaborators including an accountant at no charge. Costs appear when money moves. Card payments on invoices are charged at a percentage plus a fixed fee, historically around 2.9 percent plus 60 cents in the United States. Bank transfers and direct debit style payments carry a percentage fee with a minimum charge, which is usually cheaper than a card for large invoices. Payroll, advisory services and any paid premium features are separate subscriptions. Wave has moved some capabilities behind paid add-ons over the years, so the free and paid boundary should be verified against the current plan page.

The limitations matter once a business grows. Inventory tracking is minimal, with no stock valuation, purchase orders or reorder points, so a product business needs a dedicated inventory tool. Project accounting exists but lacks the depth of profitability reporting found in mid-market software. Payments and payroll are available only in a limited set of countries, making Wave impractical for a business with employees outside North America even though the accounting works anywhere. Multi-entity consolidation, inter-company transactions and audit-grade access controls are absent. The integration marketplace is much smaller than QuickBooks or Xero, and third-party accountants are less likely to know the product. Support for free users is limited to self-service and chat, with human help positioned as a paid service.

Wave fits a solo freelancer or a business with one or two people that needs correct books, professional invoices and a way to get paid, especially in the United States or Canada where payroll is available. It fits new businesses testing whether they will survive, contractors who want their records ready for an accountant in April, and anyone for whom a monthly software fee is a real cost. It does not fit businesses holding inventory, companies with several employees in multiple countries, organizations needing multi-entity reporting, established firms whose accountants require QuickBooks or Xero files, or anyone who needs deep project profitability analysis.

Against the alternatives, the honest comparison is between a free tool that covers ninety percent of a micro business's needs and a paid tool that covers the remaining ten percent better. If a business grows past a handful of people, moving to QuickBooks or Xero later is a data migration, so starting on Wave is not free of future cost. For the period when the business is one person and a laptop, Wave removes the software subscription entirely, and its fees only appear when the business is getting paid, which is a rational trade for the segment it was designed for.

name: Wise Business
description: Wise Business gives companies local account details in several currencies, holds and converts balances at the mid-market exchange rate, pays suppliers internationally, and issues debit cards for teams. Suited to businesses that pay or get paid across borders.
overview:
Wise Business is the commercial arm of Wise plc, the cross-border money transfer company founded in London in 2010 as TransferWise by Kristo Kaarmann and Taavet Hinrikus and listed on the London Stock Exchange in 2021. A business working across borders needs to receive money in foreign currencies, hold it, convert it and pay suppliers, contractors or employees abroad, which through a conventional bank usually means foreign accounts, correspondent charges and an exchange rate with a markup buried inside it. Wise Business replaces that with one online account, published fees and the mid-market exchange rate.

The centrepiece is a multi-currency account. A business can hold and manage balances in more than forty currencies from one login and, more importantly, obtain local account details in a set of major currencies. Those details give a genuine local routing and account number for US dollars, an IBAN for euros, a sort code and account number for sterling, and equivalent identifiers for Australian, New Zealand and Canadian dollars, Singapore dollars, Hungarian forint, Turkish lira and Romanian leu, among others depending on registration country. A client in the United States can pay by domestic ACH or wire as if you were an American company, and the money lands in your Wise balance rather than being converted at an intermediary bank's rate. That removes the need for foreign subsidiaries or offshore bank relationships for many small international businesses.

The transfer mechanics are the original product. Wise prices each transfer using the mid-market exchange rate, the rate banks and currency markets trade at with each other, and charges a separate fee displayed before confirmation. There is no markup hidden inside the rate, which is the core difference from a bank or from a PayPal conversion. Fees are calculated per corridor and typically run from a fraction of a percent up to around two percent, with major routes such as dollars to euros at the low end and less liquid routes costing more. Speed depends on the corridor and how the transfer is funded. Where Wise can move money through its own local accounts in both countries rather than through SWIFT, transfers complete in minutes or the same day, while some corridors still take one to two business days. Funding can be by bank transfer, card, or local payment rails in supported countries.

Batch and recurring payments cover the operational side. A business paying fifty contractors in twenty countries can upload a single batch file or use the API to create all of those payments at once, schedule them, or set up recurring transfers for rent, salaries and subscriptions. Recipients do not need a Wise account, because payments settle into an ordinary local bank account. Every transfer produces a receipt and an audit trail, and balances move between your own currencies at the mid-market rate at any time.

The Wise Business debit card extends the account into spending. It draws from your multi-currency balances and converts at the point of sale using the same published rate, so a business with euro and dollar balances can spend both without pre-converting. Cards can be issued to team members with individual spend limits and controls, virtual cards can be generated instantly for online subscriptions, and the card works with Apple Pay and Google Pay. A monthly ATM withdrawal allowance is typically included before per-withdrawal fees apply, with allowances depending on the country of registration.

Team features and integrations make it usable as a company financial system. Roles and permissions restrict who can create, approve or view payments, and approval workflows can require a second person to authorize transfers above a threshold, which matters for fraud control in a small finance team. Transaction data exports to CSV and connects to accounting platforms such as Xero, while the Wise API and Wise Platform let software companies embed transfers into their own products.

Compared with its competitors, Wise differentiates on pricing transparency rather than breadth of banking services. A traditional bank offers credit, cash handling and in-branch service, but adds a markup to the exchange rate, charges SWIFT and correspondent fees, and takes days to settle. PayPal moves money internationally and holds balances, but converts at its own rate with a spread usually several times a Wise fee. Revolut Business offers a similar account and cards, but applies exchange rate limits and weekend surcharges on lower tiers. Airwallex competes most directly on the same proposition with more emphasis on platform APIs and card issuing for technology companies. Payoneer is strong with marketplace sellers such as Amazon and Upwork vendors, and brokers such as OFX beat Wise on very large single transfers where a human negotiates the rate. Wise wins on cost clarity and on receiving money like a local.

Pricing has three parts. Opening and holding a Wise Business account is free, as is holding balances in the supported currencies. Activating local receiving account details can carry a one-time fee that varies by registration country, so it should be checked during signup. Each transfer costs a small percentage plus a fixed fee, both shown before confirmation, and receiving into your local account details may carry a small inbound fee in some currencies. Card issuance may involve a delivery charge, and a paid plan tier for larger teams adds extra users and higher limits. Wise publishes fees per corridor on its website, and because they change with market conditions and regulation, the fee for a route should be checked there.

The limitations are structural and worth stating plainly. Wise is not a bank. Depending on the jurisdiction it operates as an electronic money institution or a licensed money transmitter, so customer funds are safeguarded in segregated accounts or low-risk liquid assets rather than held as insured deposits. Protection schemes differ by country, and some US products involve partner banks with pass-through deposit insurance arrangements that need confirming for a specific balance. There is no lending, no overdraft and no business loan. Cash deposits and cheque handling are not supported, and certain entity types, industries and countries are restricted during onboarding, which involves verification that can take days. Card availability, plan features and supported currencies vary by registration country, and support is app and chat based with no branch network.

Wise Business fits remote-first companies paying contractors in several countries, e-commerce sellers receiving marketplace payouts in foreign currencies, agencies billing overseas clients, software companies with international customers, startups that want to hold a few currencies without foreign bank accounts, and anyone whose bank quotes a conversion spread exceeding the Wise fee. It does not fit businesses that need credit facilities or overdrafts, cash-heavy operations, companies whose regulators or investors require funds to sit at a chartered bank, purely domestic businesses with no foreign currency exposure, or organizations that need a full treasury relationship from one institution.

Against the alternatives, Wise is rarely the only financial provider a business uses. The common pattern is a domestic bank for payroll, taxes and credit, with Wise Business handling international receiving, currency holding and outbound payments where its fees are lower. On that narrow job it is one of the cheapest and most transparent options available.

name: Zoho Books
description: Zoho Books is online accounting software covering invoicing, expense tracking, bank reconciliation, inventory, project billing, and tax reporting. Integrates with the wider Zoho suite and offers a free plan for businesses under an annual revenue threshold.
overview:
Zoho Books is the accounting application inside Zoho Corporation's suite of business software. Zoho was founded in 1996, is headquartered in Chennai with a significant US presence in Austin, Texas, and publishes more than fifty applications covering CRM, finance, collaboration, HR and IT management. Zoho Books is the general ledger at the centre of that, handling invoicing, banking, payables, expenses and financial reporting. It is aimed at freelancers, small businesses and the accountants who serve them, and it is published in regional editions for the United States, United Kingdom, India, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, Australia, Canada, South Africa and a global version, each with local tax rules and reporting formats built in.

The accounting engine is a proper double-entry system. Transactions post to a configurable chart of accounts, bank and card accounts connect to feeds that import transactions automatically, and a reconciliation view matches those imports against statements. Journals can be entered manually, recurring journals can be scheduled, and multi-currency transactions are supported with exchange rates applied per transaction and unrealized gain and loss handling at period end. Fixed asset tracking with depreciation schedules is included, which is a feature many small-business tools omit. Reporting covers profit and loss, balance sheet, cash flow, trial balance, general ledger, receivable and payable ageing, tax summaries, budgets against actuals, and custom reports built by dragging dimensions onto a layout.

Tax handling is where the regional editions earn their keep. The UK edition supports Making Tax Digital for VAT with direct submission to HMRC. The Indian edition handles GST registration details, GST-compliant invoice formats and return summaries. The US edition manages sales tax rates by jurisdiction, applies them to invoices and produces filing summaries. Because these rules differ fundamentally between countries, Zoho runs separate editions rather than one global product with a tax toggle, so the correct edition must be chosen at signup and cannot simply be switched later.

Invoicing and receivables are the most-used surface.
