Zoho Books creates estimates that convert to invoices, sales orders for fulfillment flows, retainer invoices for advance payments, recurring invoices on any interval, and deposit or partial payment handling. Templates are customizable with branding and per-customer layouts, and a client portal gives each customer a login to view their own invoices and statements. Payment reminders automate chasing, late fees can be applied by rule, credit notes and refunds are handled natively, and documents can be emailed or shared as links. Payments can be accepted through gateways including Stripe, PayPal and Square as well as Zoho's own payments product, so the gateway fee is separate from the subscription.

Payables and expenses complete the cycle. Bills are entered or captured from supplier emails, matched against purchase orders and scheduled for payment runs. Vendor credits, expense reports with receipt attachments, employee reimbursements and multi-level approval workflows are supported, with routing configurable by amount, category or user. Zoho Expense integrates for detailed travel and expense management where the built-in features fall short.

Automation and extensibility distinguish Zoho Books from tools in the same price band. Workflow rules trigger actions on conditions, such as emailing an invoice when it is marked sent or creating a task when a payment is late. Custom fields and modules can be added to most records. The API and webhooks let external systems read and write accounting data, and Deluge, Zoho's scripting language, allows logic no rule builder covers. Zoho Creator can extend Books with bespoke applications sharing the same data, so a small business can automate its own edge cases without buying an enterprise system.

The ecosystem is the strategic reason to consider Zoho at all. Books shares contacts, items and invoices with Zoho CRM so a sales pipeline and a ledger stay in sync, alongside Zoho Inventory for stock control, Zoho Subscriptions for recurring billing, Zoho Commerce for storefronts, Zoho Analytics for reporting across sources, Zoho Desk for support and Zoho Practice for accounting firms managing client books. Zoho One bundles all of it at a single per-employee price, which is usually cheaper than buying accounting separately for a company already using several Zoho apps.

Compared with competitors, Zoho Books competes on price and integration depth rather than on accountant familiarity. QuickBooks Online has the largest integration ecosystem and the largest pool of accountants who know it, but it charges per tier, has raised prices repeatedly and caps transaction volumes on lower plans. Xero is well regarded in the UK, Australia and New Zealand with strong bank reconciliation, but has no true free plan. FreshBooks is invoicing-first and prices per user. Wave gives the accounting away free and monetizes payments and payroll, with less automation. Sage has long-standing UK strength and mid-market products above this tier. Zoho's advantage is a free entry tier and a low subscription price that includes automation, a client portal and API access that rivals charge extra for.

Pricing is tiered per organization rather than per user on the lower plans. A free plan is available for businesses with annual revenue below 50,000 US dollars, covering one user plus an accountant with invoicing, banking, expense tracking and basic reporting. Above that come Standard, Professional, Premium, Elite and Ultimate plans, running roughly from fifteen to two hundred and forty dollars per month on annual billing in the United States, with each step raising the user limit and adding inventory, multi-currency, project tracking, custom reports, automation depth and finally dedicated support. Regional pricing differs and tiers are revised periodically, so current figures should be confirmed on Zoho's pricing page. Payment processing fees and payroll are additional.

The limitations are real. Inventory inside Books handles items, prices and stock counts, but batch tracking, multi-warehouse and serialization require Zoho Inventory, adding cost and a second product to learn. There is no native US payroll, so payroll means an integration. Multi-entity consolidation is limited compared with mid-market systems. US sales tax automation is less complete than a dedicated tax engine, so high-volume sellers across many states still need extra tooling. The breadth of settings creates a learning curve, and the interface rewards configuration rather than working well untouched. Exports exist, but migrating to another platform is a manual project. Support response times vary by plan tier.

Zoho Books fits freelancers and micro businesses that want correct double-entry books without a subscription, small companies already using Zoho CRM or Zoho Inventory, international businesses needing a locally compliant edition for VAT, GST or sales tax, accounting practices managing many small clients through Zoho Practice, and technically minded owners who want API access and custom functions. It does not fit US businesses that need payroll in the same product, groups requiring consolidated multi-entity reporting, companies whose accountants insist on QuickBooks files, or organizations that want software they never have to configure.

Against the alternatives, the choice is usually between ecosystem and familiarity. If your accountant lives in QuickBooks and your integrations are already built for it, switching saves little. If you are starting fresh, or already use several Zoho products, then Zoho Books offers a free entry point, low paid tiers and automation depth that is hard to match at the price, and it grows into a full business suite without a migration.

name: Sage
description: Sage offers accounting software across company sizes, from Sage Business Cloud Accounting for small firms to Sage 50 for desktop-led accounting and Sage Intacct for multi-entity mid-market finance teams. Covers general ledger, invoicing, cash flow, payroll, and financial reporting.
overview:
Sage is a British accounting and business software company whose products span from a one-person freelancer filing their first tax return to a multinational finance team closing thirty subsidiaries. The Sage Group was founded in 1981 in Newcastle upon Tyne, is listed on the London Stock Exchange and a constituent of the FTSE 100, and grew largely through acquisition, which is why the portfolio overlaps. For most buyers the relevant lines are Sage Business Cloud Accounting for small businesses, Sage 50 Accounting for companies needing heavier desktop-era functionality with cloud access, and Sage Intacct for mid-market finance departments. Above those sit Sage X3 for enterprise resource planning and manufacturing, plus payroll, HR and payments products.

Sage Business Cloud Accounting runs in a browser with mobile apps for iOS and Android. It handles bank feeds, invoice and quote creation with customizable templates, expense capture through receipt photos, sales tax and VAT handling, cash flow tracking, standard financial statements and multiple users depending on the tier. Payments can be taken through integrations with Stripe and PayPal or through Sage's own payments offering. The higher tiers add project tracking with profitability by job, inventory management and multiple currencies, so the tier choice is a question of how much of the business must be modeled in the ledger.

Sage 50 Accounting has the longest lineage, descending from the desktop software that made Sage a household name among British and American small businesses. It is sold with cloud-connected features that allow remote access and sharing with an accountant while retaining a Windows desktop application at its core. Its strengths are depth rather than convenience: larger transaction volumes, more complex inventory including assemblies and serialized stock, job costing, multiple departments and companies with consolidation, and stronger controls over period closing and audit trails. For a manufacturer, wholesaler or construction subcontractor that has outgrown cloud-only software but does not need a full enterprise resource planning system, Sage 50 occupies the middle ground, with remote access dependent on the accompanying cloud service.

Sage Intacct is a different class of product and the reason Sage competes in the mid-market. It is a cloud financial management system built around dimensions rather than a rigid chart of accounts, so a single transaction can carry entity, department, location, project, customer and custom dimensions at once and be reported on any of them without duplicating accounts. That makes multi-entity consolidation, inter-company transactions, multi-currency translation and dimensional reporting manageable at a scale where spreadsheets fail. It includes automated close, revenue recognition aligned with ASC 606, cash management, purchasing, projects, contracts, order management and self-built dashboards, with industry editions for nonprofits, construction, healthcare, professional services and software. Its open API and prebuilt integrations with CRM, payroll and business intelligence tools make it a system of record, and its audit trail suits companies preparing for an external audit.

Around these sit the adjacent products. Sage Payroll and Sage HR handle compensation, benefits and people data, with availability varying substantially between the United Kingdom, United States and Canada. Sage X3 is the enterprise resource planning system for larger manufacturers and distributors. Sage Network and related payment products let businesses pay suppliers and receive funds inside the accounting workflow. Sage Copilot applies generative artificial intelligence across the products and is being rolled out progressively. A large partner channel means many implementations are delivered by resellers.

Compared with its competitors, Sage occupies an unusual position because it competes in more than one segment. In small business accounting its rivals are QuickBooks Online, Xero, Zoho Books, Wave and FreshBooks. QuickBooks has the largest accountant ecosystem and integration marketplace in the United States and Xero is strong in the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand, and both are more familiar to bookkeepers than Sage's cloud product, which is often chosen by existing Sage customers. In the mid-market, Sage Intacct competes with Oracle NetSuite, which bundles a wider enterprise resource planning scope, and with Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central for companies invested in the Microsoft stack. Intacct is generally regarded as stronger on pure financial management and multi-entity reporting, while NetSuite and Business Central cover more operational ground.

Pricing across the three lines is structured very differently, and only the smallest is published cleanly. Sage Business Cloud Accounting in the United States is sold in Start, Pro and Premium tiers, historically around ten, seventeen and twenty-five dollars per month respectively, frequently with a discounted introductory period, and a combined tier bundling payroll costs more. The Start tier is deliberately limited, restricting invoice volume and omitting multi-currency, so growing businesses usually choose Pro or higher. Sage 50 is sold as an annual subscription per company with Pro, Premium and Quantum tiers, typically running several hundred dollars per year depending on tier and payroll. Sage Intacct is not publicly priced. It is sold through a quote process with annual contracts commonly beginning in the low thousands of dollars per month for a single entity, increasing with entities, users and modules, plus implementation services usually delivered by a partner. These figures change and vary by region, so all three should be confirmed with Sage or a reseller.

The limitations follow from the portfolio structure. Product overlap confuses buyers and the lines are not automatically portable, so migrating from Business Cloud Accounting to Sage 50 or Intacct is a data project rather than an upgrade path. There is no free plan, only trials, which puts Sage behind Wave and Zoho Books for a business that wants to start at zero cost. The Start tier is too restrictive for real use and Sage 50 remains Windows-centric. Sage Intacct implementations require a partner, take weeks to months, and are not something a small business adopts casually. The third-party integration marketplace is smaller than QuickBooks Online's, particularly in North America. Support quality varies between direct Sage and reseller support, and add-ons for payroll, payments and HR each carry their own subscription.

Sage fits different buyers at different points. Business Cloud Accounting fits an established small business, particularly in the United Kingdom or Ireland where the brand and accountant familiarity are strongest, that wants standard bookkeeping with sales tax or VAT handling. Sage 50 fits a business with inventory, job costing or multiple companies that wants desktop depth with cloud access. Sage Intacct fits finance teams from roughly ten million dollars in revenue upwards, companies with multiple entities or currencies, nonprofits and professional services firms with specialized reporting needs, and businesses preparing for investment or audit. None of them fit a freelancer who needs free software or an early-stage startup without a finance function.

Against the alternatives, the decision is usually about which segment you are buying for. For micro businesses, QuickBooks, Xero, Wave and Zoho Books all offer easier starts at lower cost. For mid-market finance teams, Sage Intacct is one of the strongest dedicated financial management systems available and frequently beats a full enterprise resource planning suite on implementation speed and reporting depth. The value of Sage as a whole is that a company can begin on the small business product and move up to Intacct as it grows, provided it accepts that the move is a re-implementation.

name: Copilot Money
description: Copilot Money is a subscription personal finance app that aggregates bank, card, investment, and loan accounts, categorizes transactions, tracks budgets and net worth, and surfaces cash flow insights. Launched on Apple platforms before expanding to web and Android.
overview:
Copilot Money is a subscription personal finance app that aggregates bank accounts, cards, loans and investments into a single dashboard for budgeting, cash flow analysis and net worth tracking. It is aimed at people who want automatic transaction import and a well-designed interface, and who are willing to pay an annual fee rather than use an ad-supported product. The app started life as an iPhone-only project and still treats Apple platforms as its primary target, which shapes both its polish and its limitations.

Availability is the first thing to understand about Copilot. It runs natively on iPhone, iPad and Mac, with an Apple Watch app and home screen widgets, and a web version became available in late 2025. There is no Android app. For households where one partner uses Android, that is a hard constraint rather than a minor inconvenience, because the subscription is tied to a platform the second person cannot install.

Account connections are handled through third-party data aggregators. Copilot uses Plaid for the majority of institutions, and falls back to Mastercard Data Connect, MX and Akoya for banks that Plaid does not cover. The vendor states that it can reach more than ten thousand US financial institutions, with direct integrations for a handful of specific services such as Apple Card, Venmo and Coinbase. Connections are read-only, meaning the app can see balances and transactions but cannot move money out of an account. Coverage is heavily weighted toward the United States, and users with accounts at non-US banks should assume they will be entering those balances manually if they can track them at all.

Budgeting in Copilot works at the category level rather than through an envelope or zero-based method. Transactions are categorized automatically as they arrive, and the app learns from corrections over time, so a merchant that is miscategorized once tends to be filed correctly afterwards. Users set monthly budgets per category, and the app reports how much of each budget remains alongside a rolling view of spending by category. There is also a mechanism for excluding individual transactions from budget calculations, which matters for reimbursements, transfers and one-off purchases that would otherwise distort the picture.

Cash flow is where Copilot puts most of its analytical weight. The app separates money coming in from money going out, identifies recurring transactions, and forecasts upcoming bills and income so users can see what a month is likely to look like before it finishes. Recurring transactions can be confirmed, edited or marked as irregular. Subscription detection is included, surfacing repeating card charges with their amounts and renewal dates, which is the feature most often cited as the reason people keep the subscription after the novelty of net worth tracking wears off.

Net worth and investment tracking round out the picture. Linked accounts roll into a total net worth figure with historical trend lines, and investment accounts show holdings, allocation and performance over time. This is useful for a general view of whether savings are growing, but it is not a substitute for the deeper portfolio analysis offered by products built specifically for investors, which model fee drag, expected returns and retirement projections in far more detail.

The Apple-first approach shows up in small details that add up. Widgets on the home screen and Lock Screen display balances and remaining budget without opening the app, the Watch app gives a glanceable summary, and the software respects system features like Face ID, dark mode and Shortcuts automation. Performance on Apple hardware is generally good, with large transaction lists scrolling smoothly. For people who live in the Apple ecosystem, this is the main reason to choose Copilot over a cross-platform rival.

Copilot does not sell user financial data and does not display advertising or push product referrals inside the app. The business model is the subscription itself, which removes the conflict of interest present in free apps that earn money by recommending credit cards and loans. The company publishes its data handling and aggregation partners openly, and the app requires no connection to accounts that a user does not want to link.

Pricing is simple but not cheap. There is a single paid plan at $95 per year or $13 per month, with no free tier and no split between basic and premium feature sets. Paying annually saves roughly $61 compared with the monthly rate. A free trial of about one month is offered, and it requires payment details up front and converts automatically to a paid subscription unless cancelled, so the trial needs to be diarised. Subscribers who never let their plan lapse keep whatever price they originally signed up at, which means older users may pay less than the current listed rate.

The limitations follow directly from the design decisions. No Android app excludes a large share of households. US-centric bank coverage limits usefulness for anyone with significant finances outside the United States, and even inside the US, aggregator connections break periodically and require re-authentication, a problem shared by every app in this category rather than one specific to Copilot. The subscription-only model means the app stops being useful the moment payment lapses, and there is no export-and-keep ownership option. Budgeting is category-based rather than zero-based, so people who want every dollar assigned a job before the month starts will find the model too loose.

Copilot fits Apple users with US bank accounts who want automatic aggregation, a clean interface, subscription detection and cash flow forecasting, and who are comfortable paying roughly $95 a year for software with no advertising. It does not fit Android households, people who need a free tool, users with mostly non-US finances, or anyone who wants rigorous envelope-style budgeting or detailed investment and retirement planning.

Compared with Monarch Money, Copilot offers a more refined Apple-native experience but weaker cross-platform reach, since Monarch ships iOS, Android and web from the same subscription and allows multiple household members to share one plan. Compared with Empower Personal Dashboard, Copilot is better at day-to-day budgeting while Empower is stronger on portfolio analysis and costs nothing to use, in exchange for advisory sales calls. Compared with EveryDollar and PocketGuard, Copilot is less prescriptive and less cheap, but it imports transactions automatically at every tier. For someone already paying for Apple hardware and services, the platform fit often decides the question in Copilot's favour.

name: Empower
description: Empower Personal Dashboard is a free tool tracking net worth, investments, budgets, and cash flow by aggregating bank and brokerage accounts. Includes retirement planning, investment check-up, and fee analysis, with paid advisory services layered on top.
overview:
Empower Personal Dashboard is a free financial aggregation and planning tool that tracks net worth, cash flow, budgets and investment portfolios in one place. It is the continuation of Personal Capital, a well-known independent wealth tracking product that Empower Retirement acquired in 2020 and later folded into its own brand. The dashboard serves people who hold a meaningful amount of assets across several institutions and want a consolidated view without paying for software, and it also functions as the front door to the company's paid advisory business.

The core of the product is net worth tracking. Users link checking and savings accounts, credit cards, mortgages, auto loans, student loans, brokerage accounts, 401(k) and IRA plans, and even illiquid holdings such as property or private equity entered manually. Linked balances update automatically, and the dashboard shows a total figure with a historical trend line, so changes in wealth are visible month to month rather than only when someone builds a spreadsheet. For households with assets scattered across five or ten institutions, this consolidation is the single most valuable thing the tool does.

Investment analysis is the second strength and the clearest inheritance from Personal Capital. The Investment Checkup tool reviews the asset allocation across every linked account, compares it against a recommended target based on age and risk tolerance, and flags drift. Holdings are broken down by asset class, sector, geography and individual position, including a view through company stock and concentrated positions that people often forget they hold. A Fee Analyzer reports the expense ratios and advisory fees embedded in mutual funds and retirement plans, which is a genuinely useful piece of information that most brokerage statements bury.

Planning tools extend beyond reporting into projection. The Retirement Planner models income from savings, Social Security and pensions against expected spending, and runs market simulations to estimate the probability that money lasts through a chosen retirement age. A Savings Planner does the same for shorter goals. Users can test scenarios such as buying a house, paying for college or retiring three years early, and see the effect on the projection. These tools are more sophisticated than anything offered by the budgeting apps in the same category, though they are also more abstract and less actionable on a weekly basis.

Budgeting and cash flow exist but are not the centre of gravity. The dashboard categorizes transactions, shows income against spending, and tracks category-level spending over time. It is adequate for spotting trends and unusual months, but it lacks the forward-looking, every-dollar-assigned discipline of zero-based budgeting apps. People whose main problem is overspending between paychecks will generally get more from a dedicated budgeting tool than from Empower.

Account connections rely on third-party aggregation, with read-only access so that no money can be moved through the dashboard. Coverage of US financial institutions is broad, and the product is effectively US-only, since it is built around US account types, US tax-advantaged wrappers and US retirement rules. Non-US users will find most of the planning features inapplicable even where a bank link succeeds.

Empower also operates its own cash and investment products, including a high-yield cash account, and it runs a large retirement recordkeeping business for employer plans. The company has grown its advice side considerably, including the acquisition of Vanguard's Personal Advisor Services business, which made it one of the largest hybrid advice providers in the United States. This matters for users of the free dashboard because it explains how the product is funded.

The dashboard is free with no subscription, no usage limits and no advertising banners in the conventional sense. Empower states that the dashboard and its features remain free. The paid side is Empower's advisory service, which requires a minimum of $100,000 in investable assets and charges an annual fee based on assets under management, starting at 0.89% for the entry tiers and declining through lower percentages as balances rise toward and beyond $10 million. Exact current tier boundaries and percentages should be confirmed on the vendor's own fee schedule, because advisory pricing is revised periodically and depends on which service level a client is placed in.

That funding model is the principal caveat. The dashboard collects detailed information about a user's assets, and the advisory business uses linked balances to identify prospective clients. Users with substantial balances commonly report being contacted by advisors or offered a portfolio review. This is a legitimate business arrangement and it is disclosed, but it is not the same as a subscription product where the only relationship is software for money. Anyone who does not want sales contact should expect to decline it repeatedly, and should weigh that friction against the value of the free tools.

Further limitations follow from the product's focus. Transaction-level categorization is workable but less refined than in purpose-built budgeting apps, and corrections do not always propagate the way users expect. There is no envelope budgeting, no bill negotiation service and no built-in way to pay anything. Aggregator connections break and need periodic re-authentication, which is an industry-wide issue. The planning models depend on user-supplied assumptions about returns, spending and lifespan, so their outputs are only as good as the inputs.

Empower fits investors and accumulators rather than spenders. It is a good choice for someone in their thirties or older with retirement accounts, a taxable brokerage account, a mortgage and a growing balance who wants one authoritative net worth number, an allocation check and a retirement projection at no cost. It is also reasonable for people actively considering professional advice who want to evaluate Empower's own service from the inside. It is a poor fit for anyone whose immediate problem is month-to-month cash control, for people with under about $100,000 who would be below the advisory minimum and are sensitive to being marketed to, and for anyone outside the United States.

Against Monarch Money and Copilot Money, Empower trades budgeting depth and design quality for free access and materially stronger investment analytics. Against EveryDollar and PocketGuard it is not really a competitor, since those products manage spending rather than portfolios. Against a spreadsheet, it saves the manual work of updating balances and produces projections that are hard to replicate without significant effort. For portfolio-aware households that can tolerate the advisory outreach, it remains the most capable free financial dashboard available.

name: EveryDollar
description: EveryDollar is a zero-based budgeting app from Ramsey Solutions where every dollar of income is assigned a job before the month begins. The free plan uses manual entry, while Premium adds bank feeds, custom reports, and debt tracking through the Ramsey+ membership.
overview:
EveryDollar is a budgeting app from Ramsey Solutions that implements zero-based budgeting, the method where every dollar of expected income is assigned a job before the month begins and total income minus total allocations equals zero. It is aimed at individuals, couples and families in the United States who want a prescriptive, rule-driven approach to money rather than a passive record of what was already spent. The product is closely tied to the wider Ramsey system of personal finance advice, and much of its value depends on whether that philosophy suits the user.

The zero-based model is the organising principle. At the start of each month a user enters expected income, then creates budget lines for rent or mortgage, groceries, fuel, insurance, debt payments, savings and discretionary categories, allocating amounts until nothing is left unassigned. If actual income differs, allocations are adjusted so the budget still balances. The theory is that money given a purpose in advance is harder to spend carelessly than money sitting undifferentiated in a checking account. EveryDollar presents this as a single screen with a running remainder figure, which makes the discipline easy to follow and easy to see breaking.

Budget management is straightforward once the month is set up. Line items can be created, duplicated from a prior month, funded, and monitored, and transactions are recorded against them with a remaining balance shown per category. The app supports both monthly budgets and longer-horizon tracking of goals. Recurring items such as subscriptions and insurance premiums can be scheduled so they appear automatically each month. Budgets are shared across devices, which is the mechanism that makes the app workable for couples, since both partners see the same numbers and the same remaining balances.

The free tier is manual-entry only. Users type each transaction themselves, by amount and category, and can build unlimited budget lines and use the mobile and web apps at no cost. Manual entry has an argument in its favour, because entering a purchase by hand makes the spender conscious of it in a way that automatic import does not. In practice it also means that anyone who forgets to log a few days of spending ends up with a budget that no longer reflects reality, which is the most common reason free-tier users abandon the app.

Premium adds the features most people expect from a modern budgeting tool. Bank connections stream transactions from linked accounts into the budget automatically, removing the manual entry burden. Connections are read-only and use third-party aggregators including Mastercard's data connect service and Plaid, covering most major US banks and credit unions while leaving some smaller institutions and prepaid accounts unsupported. Premium also adds reporting and insights on spending trends, paycheck planning that spreads allocations across multiple pay dates within a month, a debt payoff tracker, goal setting, and a Margin Finder tool intended to show how much income is left after essentials. Beyond software features, Premium bundles access to Ramsey coaching content, including group sessions and training material built around the company's Baby Steps framework.

The Baby Steps framing is worth understanding before buying. The Ramsey method prescribes a specific order of operations, beginning with a small starter emergency fund, then debt repayment using the snowball method where the smallest balance is attacked first regardless of interest rate, then a larger emergency reserve, then retirement saving at a defined percentage of income, then college funding, then mortgage payoff. EveryDollar's goals and roadmap features are structured around these steps. The debt snowball is behaviourally effective for many people and mathematically slower than prioritising the highest interest rate, and users who prefer the mathematical approach will find the app's assumptions mildly irritating.

EveryDollar differs from competitors mainly in how directive it is. YNAB uses a similar envelope-style allocation philosophy but with a steeper learning curve and a higher price. Monarch Money and Copilot Money are cash flow and net worth tools that report on spending rather than requiring a pre-committed plan. PocketGuard computes a single safe-to-spend number instead of asking the user to allocate each dollar. EveryDollar sits closest to YNAB in method while being considerably simpler to learn, and it carries a strong content and coaching layer that the purely software-focused alternatives do not attempt.

Pricing splits into the free manual tier and the paid Premium tier. Premium has been listed at $79.99 per year or $17.99 per month, with a trial period of around two weeks before the first charge. Ramsey Solutions also sells Premium as part of its broader Ramsey+ membership, so the effective price depends on which package is bought and on promotions running at the time. Because the standalone price, the membership bundle and occasional discounted offers have all changed over the years, the current figure should be checked on the vendor's own pricing page before committing.

Limitations are substantial and mostly structural. Bank feeds are locked behind the paid tier, so free users never get automatic transactions. There is no investment tracking, no net worth view and no portfolio analysis, which means EveryDollar answers the question of how money is being spent but not the question of whether wealth is growing. Credit score monitoring is not part of the core product. Coverage is US-focused, with bank aggregation that does not extend meaningfully to other countries. Some users report aggregator connections dropping and needing re-authentication. The interface is functional rather than analytical, and reporting is lighter than in tools built around data exploration.

EveryDollar fits people who want a method handed to them. It suits households carrying consumer debt who want a strict plan and a payoff order, couples who need to see identical numbers on two phones, and users who respond well to Ramsey's advice and want the software that matches it. It does not fit investors who want portfolio and net worth tracking, users outside the United States, people who want automatic imports without paying, or anyone who disagrees with the debt snowball and the wider Baby Steps sequencing and would find the coaching content intrusive rather than helpful.

Against YNAB, EveryDollar is cheaper, simpler and more ideological, while YNAB offers deeper education on the method itself and a more rigorous allocation workflow. Against Monarch and Copilot it trades automatic insight for manual intent, and it costs less than both at the annual rate. Against PocketGuard it demands more work from the user in exchange for more control over individual categories. Against a spreadsheet it adds device sync, shared budgets and optional bank feeds, which is the honest measure of what the subscription buys. For someone already following Ramsey's guidance, it is the natural tool. For someone looking purely for expense tracking with investment data included, it is the wrong category of product.

name: Mint
description: Mint was a free personal finance app from Intuit that aggregated accounts, categorized spending, tracked budgets and net worth, and offered credit monitoring. Intuit shut Mint down in March 2024 and moved users to Credit Karma, ending the most widely used free budgeting app of its era.
overview:
Mint was a free personal finance application that aggregated bank accounts, credit cards, loans and investments, categorized transactions automatically, and built budgets and alerts around them. It is listed here as a historical reference rather than a current recommendation, because Intuit shut the product down in March 2024 and moved its users to Credit Karma. Anyone evaluating personal finance software today should read this entry as an account of what Mint was, why it mattered for more than a decade, what happened to it, and where former users went afterwards.

Mint launched in 2007 after winning the TechCrunch40 competition, and it established the template that nearly every budgeting app since has followed. Before Mint, tracking spending across several institutions meant downloading CSV files and maintaining spreadsheets. Mint replaced that with automatic aggregation, machine categorization of merchants into buckets such as groceries, dining, fuel and utilities, and a monthly budget built on top. It was free, it worked in a browser before most competitors had mobile apps, and it required only a set of bank credentials. Intuit acquired the company in 2009 for $170 million, which brought the product into a large software publisher and gave it staying power for another fifteen years.

The feature set that made Mint sticky was broader than budgeting. Users tracked net worth across linked accounts, monitored credit scores at no cost, received alerts for unusual charges, large withdrawals, upcoming bills, overdue payments and approaching limits, and set savings goals with progress indicators. Transaction rules let people correct categorization once and have the correction persist, which over time produced an accurate personal dataset. Spending trends by category and over time turned that dataset into something analytically useful. For many households it was the first time they could see all of their money in one place without doing any work.

Mint's business model was the reason it could be free, and the reason it eventually died. The app did not charge users. It earned revenue by recommending financial products, showing offers for credit cards, loans, savings accounts and insurance inside the interface, with referral payments when a user applied. That model worked while the user base was growing and while the referral economics were attractive. It also meant the product's incentives were aligned with selling financial products rather than with budgeting depth, and it made Mint strategically redundant inside Intuit once the company owned a better vehicle for exactly that kind of recommendation.

Intuit had acquired Credit Karma in 2020 for roughly $8 billion, and Credit Karma's whole business was free tools monetized through financial product referrals. Once that acquisition was complete, Mint and Credit Karma were competing for the same job inside the same company. In November 2023 Intuit announced that Mint would be discontinued, and the shutdown took effect in March 2024. Mint users were prompted to migrate to Credit Karma, and Intuit positioned Credit Karma's cash flow and budgeting features as the replacement. Users were able to export their transaction history as CSV before access ended, which for many was the only way to preserve years of categorized spending data.

The migration was widely regarded as a downgrade, and the response shaped the current market. Credit Karma is a credit and financial-product platform first. It offered net worth style account linking and some cash flow insights, but it did not reproduce Mint's category budgets, transaction rules, bill alerts and savings goal tracking in an equivalent form. Former Mint users who wanted those features had to leave the Intuit ecosystem entirely, and a substantial number of them did, which is why several subscription budgeting apps saw their fastest growth periods immediately after the shutdown.

The destinations split into a few clear groups. Credit Karma Money and the wider Credit Karma account remained the official path and suit people who primarily want free credit monitoring and product offers. Monarch Money absorbed the largest share of committed Mint refugees, offering automatic aggregation, net worth tracking, flexible budgets, subscriptions and investment views with household sharing on one subscription. Copilot Money took a similar share among Apple users, with a strong native iOS and Mac experience and a paid-only model. PocketGuard attracted users who wanted a simple answer to how much is safe to spend this month. Empower Personal Dashboard became the default for users whose interest was net worth and portfolio analysis rather than budgeting, since its dashboard is free. EveryDollar drew users who wanted a prescriptive zero-based method with coaching content attached. Beyond those, YNAB kept its audience of envelope budgeters, Quicken Simplifi appealed to people wanting a cheaper Mint-like overview, Rocket Money focused on subscription cancellation and bill negotiation, and spreadsheet-driven options such as Tiller and Actual Budget served users who wanted ownership of their data after watching a free service disappear.

The Mint shutdown carries a lesson that is worth stating plainly, because it affects how any tool in this category should be chosen. A free product monetized through referrals or data is not free, it is paid for in a currency the user may not have intended to spend, and it can be withdrawn whenever the owner's strategy changes. Fifteen years of categorized transaction history became a CSV export. Paid subscription apps are not immune to shutting down, but their revenue depends on keeping users, which is a different set of incentives. Anyone migrating from a discontinued service should check whether the new tool exports data in an open format and how much history it will import.

There are practical consequences for anyone who still encounters Mint references. Documentation, tutorials, comparison articles and forum threads published before 2024 that recommend Mint are out of date. Mint-branded mobile apps are no longer maintained and should not be installed with bank credentials. The Mint credit score service and the Mint brand live on only as marketing language inside Credit Karma in some materials, which creates genuine confusion. A catalog entry for Mint is therefore useful for understanding the history of the category and for redirecting searches from people who are still looking for it, not for download.

As a historical product, Mint fits nobody today. As a reference point it explains the shape of the modern market, because the gap it left is exactly the gap that Monarch, Copilot, PocketGuard, Empower and EveryDollar are now competing to fill. Users who want what Mint used to give them for nothing should expect to pay somewhere in the region of $75 to $100 a year for an equivalent subscription tool, or accept a narrower free product such as Empower's dashboard that is funded by advisory referrals instead of advertising. The comparison that matters is no longer Mint against its rivals. It is which of Mint's successors best matches the specific job that Mint used to do for a given household, whether that was budgeting discipline, net worth visibility, bill alerts or credit monitoring.

name: Monarch Money
description: Monarch Money is a subscription personal finance platform built by former Mint team members. Aggregates accounts, categorizes transactions, tracks budgets, cash flow, investments, and net worth, and supports shared household access without ads or data selling.
overview:
Monarch Money is a subscription personal finance platform that combines transaction-level budgeting with net worth tracking, investment reporting and household collaboration. It was founded in 2018 by a team that included former product people from Intuit's Mint group, and it grew quickly after Intuit shut Mint down in March 2024, absorbing a large share of users looking for a direct replacement. The product runs on iOS, Android and the web, and it is available across all three from a single subscription rather than charging separately for platforms.

Account aggregation is handled through multiple third-party data providers. Monarch connects primarily through Plaid and uses MX and Finicity as alternates for institutions that Plaid does not reach, which gives it one of the broader connection success rates in the category. Links are read-only, so the software can retrieve balances and transactions but cannot initiate transfers. Coverage is strongest in the United States, and while some non-US institutions can be connected, users with primarily foreign bank accounts should expect gaps and will need manual accounts for those holdings.

Budgeting in Monarch is flexible rather than prescriptive. Users create categories, group them into higher-level buckets such as fixed costs, groceries and discretionary spending, and set monthly or rolling targets at either level. Transactions are categorized automatically as they import, with a rules engine that lets people define merchant and keyword conditions so recurring miscategorizations stop happening. Bulk editing is supported, which matters after a week of imported transactions arrives misfiled. Unlike zero-based apps, Monarch does not require income to equal allocations, so it suits people who want to monitor and adjust spending rather than commit every dollar in advance.

Cash flow reporting is where the product earns its subscription for most users. Income and spending are separated and charted over weeks, months and years, with comparisons against previous periods and against budget targets. Recurring transactions are detected and surfaced as a list, including irregular ones, and subscriptions appear with renewal dates and total annual cost. That subscription view is a common reason people sign up, since cancelling two unwanted services often pays for the year.

Net worth tracking rolls every linked and manual account into a single figure with historical trend data. Manual accounts cover property, vehicles, private equity, cryptocurrency held off-exchange and debts that no aggregator can see, which is what makes the total trustworthy rather than approximate. Investment tracking shows holdings, allocation by asset class and category, and performance over time, with gains and losses reported at both the account and the whole-portfolio level. It is not as analytically deep as a dedicated portfolio tool, but it answers the questions most households actually ask about allocation and drift.

Household collaboration is a genuine differentiator. One subscription covers multiple people in the same household, each with their own login and their own view, rather than forcing a shared password or charging per person. Partners can each categorize transactions and adjust budgets against the same underlying data. For couples who want financial visibility without giving up separate access, this removes a friction point that several competitors handle by charging extra or not handling at all.

The interface is customizable through a dashboard built from widgets, so a user who cares about net worth and another who cares about remaining grocery budget can each arrange the same product around their own priorities. Reports can be filtered by account, category, tag and date range and exported. Tags are a separate dimension from categories and support analysis that categories alone cannot express, such as tracking every expense associated with a specific trip, home renovation or client.

Monarch does not display advertising, does not sell user financial data, and does not earn referral revenue from recommending credit cards or loans inside the app. Its business model is the subscription, which aligns its incentives with keeping the software useful. The company states that it gives at least thirty days notice before any price change, a small but meaningful commitment in a category where pricing has moved often.

Pricing has a single core plan at $99.99 per year or $14.99 per month, with a seven-day free trial and no free tier. Annual billing works out at roughly $8.33 a month and saves close to $80 a year against paying monthly. Reports from 2026 describe a higher Monarch Plus tier at around $199 per year, billed annually only, which appears in third-party reviews rather than consistently on the vendor's own pricing page. Because the tier structure is recent and still settling, both the existence and the price of Plus should be confirmed on the vendor's pricing page before purchase. All subscriptions are billed in US dollars plus applicable tax.

Limitations are worth stating clearly. There is no bill payment, so the app reports on bills but does not pay them. There is no tax preparation or filing, no credit card or loan product, and no bill negotiation service. Budgeting is cash-flow oriented rather than envelope-based, which will not satisfy people who want the YNAB method specifically. Investment analysis lacks the fee modeling, retirement probability simulation and scenario planning found in products such as Empower's dashboard, which are free. The subscription-only model means the tool stops working when payment lapses, although transaction data can be exported as CSV. Bank connections still break periodically and require re-authentication, an issue shared with every app that relies on aggregators.

Monarch fits households that want one paid product covering budgeting, net worth and investments across iPhone, Android and the web, and especially couples who need separate logins on a shared financial picture. It fits former Mint users looking for the closest functional replacement. It does not fit people who need a free tool, users who want rigorous zero-based budgeting, anyone whose primary interest is retirement projection and portfolio fee analysis, or households outside the United States with limited bank coverage.

Against Copilot Money, Monarch offers Android support and multi-user household access while Copilot offers a more polished Apple-native experience. Against Empower Personal Dashboard, Monarch costs money and has no advisory sales pressure, while Empower is free and stronger on investment analytics. Against EveryDollar, Monarch reports on spending flexibly instead of demanding a pre-committed plan, and against PocketGuard it gives category-level control rather than one safe-to-spend number. Against YNAB it is easier to adopt but less methodical. Monarch occupies the general-purpose middle of the market, and its combination of cross-platform reach, household sharing and breadth of reporting is what justifies the price for the users it is built for.

name: PocketGuard
description: PocketGuard is a budgeting app that connects accounts, categorizes transactions, and calculates an in-my-pocket figure showing what can be spent after bills, goals, and necessities. Offers both a free tier and a Plus subscription.
overview:
PocketGuard is a budgeting app built around a single question: how much money can I spend today without damaging anything else. It aggregates bank accounts, cards and loans, tracks income and bills, and reduces the result to one figure the company calls In My Pocket. It suits people who find full category-by-category budgeting tedious and who want a guardrail rather than a spreadsheet, and it is available on iOS, Android and the web.

The In My Pocket calculation is the core idea and it explains everything else about the product. PocketGuard takes projected income for the month, subtracts bills that are still due, subtracts money already allocated to savings goals, subtracts expected necessities based on the user's own spending patterns, and reports what is left. The number updates as transactions arrive, so it falls after each purchase. Instead of asking a user to decide whether a restaurant bill fits within an entertainment envelope, the app answers whether it fits within the month as a whole. That framing makes the tool feel more like a speedometer than a ledger.

Account connections use third-party aggregators and are read-only, so the app can retrieve data but cannot move money. Bank and card coverage extends to the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom. Outside those three countries there are no direct connections, although the web version still supports manual accounts and manual transaction entry, so a user elsewhere can operate PocketGuard as a hand-maintained budget. This three-country limit is one of the most important practical constraints on the product and rules it out for much of the world.

Beyond the headline number, PocketGuard provides a set of supporting views. Bills are listed with due dates and amounts, and upcoming charges are folded into the safe-to-spend figure rather than sitting in a separate screen the user has to remember to check. Category budgets can be set for people who want more granularity than the single number offers. Insights break spending down by category and merchant and show trends over time. Savings goals accumulate allocations month by month and reduce the disposable figure accordingly, which is the mechanism that turns PocketGuard from an expense tracker into a saving tool.

Subscription detection is one of the more useful secondary features. Repeating card charges are identified and listed with amounts and dates, which surfaces forgotten services, free trials that converted and duplicate subscriptions. Some versions of the product have also offered help with reducing bills, though the scope of any such service and its availability vary by plan and region and should be confirmed with the vendor rather than assumed.

Recurring transactions are recognized and projected forward, so a monthly rent payment, a quarterly insurance premium or an annual membership are treated as committed money before they are actually paid. This forward projection is what makes In My Pocket defensible rather than naive, since a simple calculation based only on today's balance would be useless in the second week of any month with a large bill due.

PocketGuard differs from its competitors in how much thinking it does on the user's behalf. YNAB and EveryDollar require a plan to be built in advance and expect the user to allocate income across categories before spending. Monarch Money and Copilot Money report on cash flow and let the user draw conclusions. PocketGuard draws the conclusion itself and presents one number. The trade-off is control, because a single aggregate figure tells someone they are overspending without necessarily explaining which category is responsible, and users who want that diagnosis have to dig into the insights views.

The pricing structure is unusual in this category because it includes a permanent purchase option. There is a free tier with manual entry and reduced functionality. PocketGuard Plus has been priced at $74.99 per year or $12.99 per month, with a seven-day free trial, and a one-time Lifetime option around $149.99 that grants permanent access to Plus features without an ongoing subscription. All figures are in US dollars and the vendor notes that prices may vary by region. The Lifetime option is worth particular attention, because at roughly a year and a half of the annual price it can be the cheapest long-term route to a full-featured budgeting app anywhere in this market. Current prices and the continued availability of Lifetime should be checked on the vendor's pricing page, since promotional and permanent pricing have both changed over time.

Limitations follow from the narrow focus. Investment and portfolio tracking is minimal, and there is no net worth analysis of the kind offered by Empower or Monarch, so the app answers questions about spending but not questions about wealth. Credit score monitoring is not a core feature. There is no bill payment. Bank coverage stops at three countries. Aggregator connections break periodically and need re-authentication, which is an industry-wide condition rather than a PocketGuard defect. The single-number philosophy can also produce false comfort, since a healthy In My Pocket figure says nothing about whether spending is going to categories the user considers wasteful.

PocketGuard fits people who want a simple, automatic answer about daily spending headroom, who have bank accounts in the US, Canada or the UK, and who would rather buy software outright than subscribe indefinitely. It fits users who found Mint too shallow and YNAB too demanding, and who were left looking for something in between after the Mint shutdown in March 2024. It does not fit investors tracking a portfolio, households wanting shared multi-user access on one plan, users outside the three supported countries who need automatic bank feeds, or anyone who wants a rigorous zero-based method with coaching content attached.

Against Monarch Money and Copilot Money, PocketGuard is cheaper, simpler and less capable, trading reporting depth and net worth analysis for one clear daily number. Against EveryDollar it is automatic and undogmatic where EveryDollar is manual and prescriptive. Against Empower's free dashboard it costs money and offers far less in the way of investment analysis. Against YNAB it requires almost no learning and provides almost no methodology. The Lifetime purchase is the strongest argument for choosing it, and the three-country bank coverage is the strongest argument against. For a user in a supported country who wants a low-maintenance spending guardrail and dislikes subscriptions, PocketGuard is a reasonable and unusually affordable pick.

name: Harvest
description: Harvest is time tracking and invoicing software for agencies, consultancies, and freelancers. Tracks time by project and task, turns entries into invoices, sends payment reminders, accepts online payments, and reports on project budgets and profitability.
overview:
Harvest is web-based time tracking and invoicing software built for agencies, consultancies, studios and independent professionals who bill clients for their hours. It launched in 2006 and has remained focused on a narrow job: record time against projects and clients, capture expenses, turn both into invoices, get paid, and report on the results. It is not a project management suite and not an accounting system, and understanding that boundary explains most of what it does well.

Time tracking is the foundation. Users start and stop a timer from the web app, a browser extension, desktop apps for Mac and Windows, or mobile apps for iOS and Android, or they enter hours manually into a weekly timesheet. Every entry is attached to a client, a project and a task, the three-level structure that makes reporting meaningful later. Time can be marked billable or non-billable, and rates can be set per project, per task, per person or as a default, so a senior consultant and a junior designer can be billed at different amounts on the same project without manual arithmetic.

Project budgets turn time data into early warning. A budget can be defined in hours or in fees, tracked at project or task level, and set to alert at a chosen percentage of consumption. This prevents the most common agency loss, which is discovering a project ran over its estimate only when the final invoice is prepared. Alerts go to project managers by email and appear in the interface, so overruns are visible while there is still time to change scope.

Timesheet approval and permissions support managed teams. Projects can require approval before time is counted, team members can be restricted to assigned projects, and administrators control who sees rates, budgets and reports. This is what makes the data trustworthy enough to invoice from without a manual review pass every month.

Invoicing is where the tracked time converts into revenue. Invoices are generated from unbilled time and expenses, with quantities and rates pulled straight from the entries, and can be edited before sending. Templates are customizable with a logo, colors, notes and payment terms. Invoices are sent by email or delivered through a hosted link, and can include a payment button so clients pay by credit card. Automated reminders chase unpaid invoices on a schedule, and payments and credits are recorded so the outstanding balance stays accurate. Estimates can be converted to projects and invoices later, closing the loop from proposal to payment in one tool.

Expenses handle the reimbursable side of client work. Users photograph a receipt on the mobile app or forward a receipt email to a Harvest address, and the expense is created with the image attached. Expenses marked billable flow onto the invoice alongside time, while internal costs feed profitability reporting instead. Unrecovered expenses are one of the quietest sources of margin loss in service businesses, which is why this small feature matters.

Reporting is comparatively strong for a tool of this size. Standard reports cover teams, projects, clients, tasks, invoices, expenses, budgets and capacity, filterable by date range, client, project, person and billable status. Unbilled time and unbilled expense reports identify revenue earned but not yet invoiced, which is directly useful for cash flow forecasting at month end. Reports export to CSV and PDF, and the data is available through a documented public REST API.

Integrations connect Harvest to the tools a service business already runs. Accounting sync exists for QuickBooks Online and Xero, which removes double entry for most small firms. Work management connections include Asana, Trello and Basecamp, and Slack allows a timer to be started from a channel. Zapier extends the reach to several thousand other applications. Harvest Forecast is a separate resource scheduling and capacity planning product from the same company, sold independently but sharing client and project data.

Harvest differs from competitors by refusing scope creep. Toggl Track and Clockify compete largely on free multi-user time tracking. Everhour and Timing embed timing inside other workflows. Project management platforms such as Asana, ClickUp and Monday have added timers and invoicing as secondary features, usually thinner than a specialist product. On the invoicing side, FreshBooks and Wave target small business billing with time tracking attached rather than the reverse. Harvest's position is that a firm whose revenue depends on accurately billing hours wants both halves of that job done properly.

Pricing as of late 2026 has four tiers. The Free plan costs nothing and is limited to one seat and two active projects, viable for a solo freelancer with a small client list but not for a team. The Teams plan runs at $9 per person per month billed annually, which is $108 per seat per year, or $11 per person per month billed monthly. The Enterprise plan runs at $14 per person per month billed annually, or $168 per seat per year, and $17.50 monthly, adding advanced reporting and administrative controls. Enterprise Plus is quoted individually. Annual billing carries roughly a 20 percent discount. A 30-day free trial needs no credit card, and seats can be added mid-cycle on a prorated basis.

One change in the pricing model deserves attention. Paid plans now combine a per-seat base rate with usage-based billing, so additional invoices, projects, clients and tasks beyond the included allowances are charged according to consumption. In practice this makes monthly cost harder to predict than the old flat per-seat model, and teams migrating from legacy plans have reported substantial increases. Anyone budgeting for Harvest should model expected invoice and project volume rather than relying on the headline seat price, and confirm current allowances on the vendor's pricing page.

Limitations are mostly about what Harvest deliberately excludes. There is no double-entry ledger, no VAT or sales tax return preparation and no year-end financial statements, so an accounting package remains necessary and Harvest syncs into one rather than replacing it. There is no payroll. Project management is light, with no dependency chains or Gantt charts. Time tracking accuracy depends on people actually starting timers, and no software solves that culturally. The usage-based layer adds billing unpredictability.

Harvest fits agencies, consultancies, law and accounting practices, design studios and freelance specialists who bill hourly or per project, need client-level profitability, and want invoices to come straight out of timesheets. It fits teams of two to a few hundred that need approval workflows and per-person rates. It does not fit product companies with no billable hours, teams wanting free multi-seat tracking, or businesses needing an accounting system in the same tool.

Against FreshBooks, Harvest has stronger time capture and project budgeting while FreshBooks has deeper small-business accounting. Against Toggl Track and Clockify it costs more per seat but ties time directly to invoicing and payments. Against ClickUp or Asana it is narrower and better at the billing half of the job. Against Xero or QuickBooks it is complementary rather than competitive, since the usual setup is Harvest for time and invoices syncing into an accounting system for the books. For a service business whose margin depends on billing every hour worked, that focus is the reason Harvest has survived in a crowded market for two decades.

name: FreeAgent
description: FreeAgent is accounting software for freelancers, contractors, and micro businesses with a strong UK presence. Covers invoicing, expenses, bank reconciliation, payroll for directors and employees, VAT and Making Tax Digital submission, and cash flow forecasting.
overview:
FreeAgent is UK accounting software for freelancers, sole traders, partnerships, limited companies, landlords and micro businesses. It runs double-entry bookkeeping underneath a deliberately plain interface, so a user records an invoice or an expense without ever seeing a debit or a credit while the ledger stays correct behind the scenes. The company is based in Edinburgh and has been owned by NatWest Group since 2018, which determines who gets the product for nothing.

The free arrangement is specific and often misdescribed. FreeAgent is free for customers holding a business current account with a NatWest Group bank, meaning NatWest, Royal Bank of Scotland, Ulster Bank and Mettle. The funded licence is a full one, with the same functionality paying customers receive, applies to all company types including landlords, and lasts as long as the qualifying account is held. For Mettle the condition is at least one transaction a month. NatWest Group customers get no stripped-down version and pay nothing after a trial period.

A common misconception needs correcting directly, because comparison articles repeat it. FreeAgent is not offered free to HSBC business customers. HSBC UK provides its own embedded accounting tool, My Business Finances powered by Sage, with an introductory free period and then a monthly charge. That is a different product from a different supplier. A business banking with HSBC can still buy and use FreeAgent, but it pays the standard subscription.

For everyone else, FreeAgent is a paid subscription split by business structure, with a lower tier for sole traders and a higher one for limited companies reflecting the additional statutory work a company requires. Published list prices have been around £19 per month for sole traders and around £29 per month for limited companies, both excluding VAT, with a 50 percent discount for the first six months. Optional add-ons are priced separately and have included unlimited receipt capture through Smart Capture at roughly £5 per month and an Amazon UK connection at roughly £6 per month. Accountancy practices managing multiple clients use a separate practice arrangement. These figures are revised periodically and promotions run frequently, so current prices should be confirmed on the vendor's pricing page before purchase.

Bank feeds are the operational centre of the product. FreeAgent connects to UK bank accounts through Open Banking, importing transactions automatically and matching them against invoices, bills and expense claims. Unmatched transactions appear in a list where they can be categorized, and repeated patterns are learned. Bank reconciliation is a genuine reconciliation against the statement balance rather than a simple import, which is what makes the year-end accounts defensible.

Invoicing and estimates cover the revenue side. Invoices are created from templates with a logo and payment details, sent by email or as a hosted link, and can include a payment button so clients pay by card. Overdue invoices are chased with automated reminders, part payments are recorded and credit notes are supported. Estimates convert into invoices when work is confirmed. Multi-currency invoicing is available, which matters for freelancers with overseas clients.

Expenses are captured in several ways. Receipts can be photographed through the iOS and Android mobile apps or emailed into the account, and the Smart Capture feature extracts the amounts. Expense claims distinguish between business costs paid personally and costs paid from the business account, a distinction UK tax treatment depends on and one that simpler tools blur. Mileage can be logged and claimed, and expenses feed into the profit and loss position and the tax calculations automatically.

Tax handling is where FreeAgent differentiates itself most clearly from generic bookkeeping tools. It is recognised software for Making Tax Digital for VAT, so returns are submitted directly to HMRC without a bridging tool. It prepares Self Assessment returns for sole traders and partnerships and produces corporation tax estimates for limited companies. A Tax Timeline shows upcoming filing and payment dates with amounts, and running estimates of tax liability are maintained throughout the year rather than appearing as a surprise after year end.

Payroll is included rather than sold as an add-on. FreeAgent runs UK payroll for employees and directors, handling PAYE, tax codes, payslips, Full Payment Submissions to HMRC, and the year-end P60 and P45 process. Many competing packages charge per employee or per payroll run, so bundling payroll into the base subscription materially changes the real cost for a limited company with a director on payroll, which describes a large share of UK micro businesses.

Project tracking and time recording support service businesses. Time can be logged against projects and clients and billed through invoices, and project profitability reports show income against time and expense costs. This is lighter than a dedicated time tracking product such as Harvest, but sufficient for a freelancer or small consultancy billing hours.

Reporting covers the statutory and managerial basics, including profit and loss, balance sheet, cash flow, aged debtors and creditors, VAT summaries and tax estimates. Reports are exportable, and accountants can be given access to the books. FreeAgent also runs a practice offering so accountancy firms can manage multiple client companies from one dashboard, and its large accountant user base means a business can hand its books to an adviser without a migration.

How FreeAgent differs from its rivals comes down to jurisdiction and price. Xero and QuickBooks Online UK are broader, more extensible platforms with larger app marketplaces, more inventory and multi-entity features, and higher entry prices that rise with headcount. Sage and Zoho Books occupy adjacent positions. What none of them can match is a genuinely free full-featured licence for customers of the owner's own banks. For a NatWest, RBS, Ulster Bank or Mettle customer the effective price is zero, which removes the usual cost comparison entirely.

Limitations are real. It is UK-focused, built around HMRC rules, UK payroll and UK banking, so it is the wrong tool for a business filing in another jurisdiction, though a separate US edition with a different feature set and pricing exists and should be evaluated independently rather than assumed equivalent. Inventory and stock management is not a strength, so product businesses with meaningful stockholding will outgrow it. Complex payroll scenarios, multi-entity consolidation and heavy custom reporting are better served by larger platforms. The integration ecosystem is smaller than Xero's.

FreeAgent fits UK sole traders, freelancers, contractors, landlords and one-to-ten-person limited companies that need bookkeeping, VAT filing, Self Assessment or corporation tax estimates and payroll in one place. It fits NatWest Group banking customers above all, for whom it is free. It does not fit businesses outside the UK, companies with substantial inventory, or firms needing deep project delivery tooling.

Against Xero and QuickBooks Online, FreeAgent is narrower and cheaper, often free, and stronger on bundled payroll and direct UK tax filing, while weaker on integrations and scalability. Against Sage it is generally easier for a non-accountant to operate day to day. Against Harvest it is complementary, since Harvest handles time and client invoicing while FreeAgent handles the books and the tax. For a UK micro business banking with NatWest Group there is little financial reason to look further. For everyone else, the question is whether bundled payroll and HMRC filing are worth the subscription against a larger platform that will still fit in five years.

name: 15Five
description: 15Five is a performance management platform built around weekly check-ins, one-on-one agendas, goal tracking, feedback, and engagement surveys. Aimed at managers and HR teams that want continuous performance conversations instead of a single annual review cycle.
overview:
15Five is a continuous performance management platform built on the premise that short weekly conversations produce better outcomes than an annual evaluation. The name describes the intended time cost, fifteen minutes for an employee to write a check-in and five minutes for a manager to read and respond to it. The product serves people teams and line managers at organizations roughly between fifty and a few thousand employees, and it bundles check-ins, one-on-ones, goals, review cycles, engagement surveys and manager coaching into one system rather than selling them as disconnected point tools.

The weekly check-in is the core mechanic. Employees answer a configurable set of questions each week, typically covering priorities, blockers, mood, work-life balance and a free-text field for anything else a manager should know. Managers see responses in a queue, reply inline, promote topics into the next one-on-one and track response rates over time. Because the question set is editable, teams can add questions tied to a reorganization or a new policy and retire questions that have stopped producing signal.

One-on-one management sits directly on top of those check-ins. Each manager and report share a persistent agenda that accumulates topics, decisions and action items. Unfinished items roll forward automatically, so a recurring meeting retains a written history of what was discussed and what was promised. The platform notifies managers when meetings are skipped repeatedly and serves coaching prompts from a library of management scenarios such as delivering critical feedback, addressing burnout or running a first review with a new report.

Goals give the conversations something concrete to point at. Companies define objectives at the organization level and cascade them to departments, teams and individuals, with key results attached and progress tracked as a percentage. Updates can be requested on a schedule, and goal status appears inside check-ins and review cycles so that performance discussions reference written commitments instead of recollection. Both OKR-style and traditional goal models are supported without forcing a single methodology.

Review cycles are where the formal evaluation happens. The signature cycle is called the Best-Self Review, which asks an employee to describe their strengths and recent accomplishments before a manager writes an assessment. Cycles support self-review, manager review, peer feedback, upward feedback on managers and full 360 reviews, with configurable rating scales or no numeric ratings at all. Reviewers get calibration views, people leaders see completion status across the company, and drafting assistance is available to reduce biased or vague language while still requiring a human to write the final text.

Engagement measurement is the other half of the platform. Teams run short pulse surveys weekly or monthly alongside larger annual and lifecycle surveys covering engagement, inclusion, wellbeing and manager effectiveness. Results are reported with eNPS-style scoring, cuts by department, location, tenure and demographic group, historical trend lines and comparison against a benchmark database drawn from other customers. Survey output feeds into action planning, where managers select one or two focus areas and the system tracks whether follow-up commitments were actually made, which is the step most survey programs quietly abandon.

Reporting and integrations determine whether adoption creates extra administrative work. People analytics dashboards combine engagement scores, check-in sentiment, goal progress, review completion and turnover risk, and every view can be filtered by team or tenure band. 15Five connects to Slack and Microsoft Teams so check-ins are requested and answered where people already work, and it syncs with common HRIS and payroll systems so employee records, managers and reporting lines stay current without manual imports. Single sign-on and automated user provisioning are available for organizations that require them.

The competitive difference is the emphasis on manager behavior rather than HR process administration. Lattice, Leapsome and Culture Amp offer overlapping feature lists, but 15Five consistently frames the product around the recurring manager-employee conversation and ships coaching content to support it. It is also less configuration-heavy than Lattice, which shortens time to value for a people team without a dedicated administrator, and it usually costs less than enterprise performance suites. The trade-off is a smaller engagement benchmark library than Culture Amp and less developed compensation planning and analytics than Lattice.

Pricing has historically been published per user per month with annual-only billing. For several years the vendor listed three tiers, an Engage tier covering check-ins, one-on-ones and surveys at roughly four dollars per user per month, a Focus tier adding goals and review cycles at roughly ten dollars, and a Total Platform tier including career development and compensation tooling at roughly fourteen dollars. The company has since shifted toward bundled packages and quote-based deals for larger customers, so those figures are indicative only and should be confirmed on the vendor pricing page before any budget is built on them.

The main limitations are behavioral rather than technical. A weekly check-in program only generates data if managers respond, and organizations with inconsistent management practices will see low response rates and empty sentiment trends. Review cycles are less flexible for complex calibration and compensation linkage than Lattice or an HCM-integrated setup. The analytics layer is adequate for a people team but is not a warehouse-grade product, and heavy customization of survey logic or review workflows can require paid implementation support.
