Collision detection shows when a colleague is already writing a reply, which eliminates the specific and common failure of two agents answering the same customer within minutes of each other. Statuses such as open, pending, resolved and closed give a conversation a lifecycle, so a thread that is waiting on the customer or on an internal answer is distinguishable from one that needs action, and a queue can be measured rather than eyeballed.

Internal collaboration happens through notes on a conversation, visible to the team and invisible to the customer, so an agent can ask a colleague for help, flag a sensitive account or hand over context without forwarding an email and starting a separate thread. Mentions notify specific people. This is functionally similar to the chat-in-thread model in Missive and to comments in Front, and it is the feature that turns a shared mailbox into a collaborative workspace rather than a source of confusion.

Service level agreements formalise response and resolution expectations. Targets are configured by priority, by group or by channel, timers run against conversations, warnings fire before a breach, and breaches are escalated and reported. For a business with contractual support commitments, or one that simply wants to know whether it answers promptly, this converts an impression into a number that can be managed. Reporting covers response time, first-response time, resolution time, volume by agent and by group, backlog and satisfaction, with the ability to compare periods and teams. This is the layer that allows a manager to identify a bottleneck rather than guess at one.

Automation removes repetitive decisions. Rules evaluate conditions on an incoming message, including sender domain, recipient address, subject and body content, attachments and time of day, and perform actions such as assigning to a person or group, applying a status or tag, sending an auto-response, adding a note or triggering an escalation. Collision and duplication rules prevent repeated work. The automation capability is shallower than Front's rules engine and nowhere near a workflow platform, but it covers the routing and acknowledgement patterns a small team actually needs, and it is configured in minutes rather than in a project.

Channels extend beyond email. Voice support allows calls to be handled and logged alongside email conversations. WhatsApp, which is a primary business messaging channel across much of the world, can be connected so those conversations appear in the same queue with the same assignment, status and reporting. Live chat via a website widget brings on-site conversations into Gmail. This matters because a team whose customers split between email, WhatsApp and chat otherwise maintains three systems, and the alternative to consolidation is not efficiency but messages being missed.

A knowledge base publishes help articles for self-service, which is the highest-leverage intervention in support economics because a deflected ticket costs nothing while an answered one costs an agent's time. Articles can be surfaced to agents while they write a reply, so repeated answers become a link rather than a fresh composition, and repeated links become a signal that an article needs improving.

Artificial intelligence features assist with drafting responses based on conversation history and knowledge base content, summarising long threads so an agent picking up a conversation gains context quickly, translating, and categorising or routing incoming messages. The honest assessment of AI drafting in support is that it is genuinely useful for routine queries and risky for anything requiring judgment or carrying commercial consequence, and teams that publish AI drafts without human review produce confident wrong answers. Hiver positions this as assistance to an agent rather than as autonomous resolution, which is the more defensible design for a small team.

Integrations connect the help desk to the rest of the stack. Salesforce, HubSpot and Zoho CRM sync conversation history to account and contact records, so a sales or account team sees every support interaction without leaving the CRM. Jira, Zendesk, Slack, Microsoft Teams, Trello, Asana and Zoho Desk allow escalation into engineering or into a workflow tool with a link back to the conversation. Shopify, Stripe and other commerce and payment tools attach order and transaction context, which removes the most common support question of what did this customer actually buy. An API and webhooks support custom integration. Because Hiver operates on Gmail, Google Workspace-native behaviour including labels, filters, signatures and search continues to work, which is a practical advantage over a platform that abstracts the mailbox away.

Against competitors, Front is the strongest collaborative shared inbox and customer communication platform, with a deeper rules engine, broader channel coverage including SMS and social, more mature analytics, a larger integration marketplace and native desktop applications, at a higher per-seat price and with email ingested into its own platform rather than left in Gmail. Missive offers internal chat in email threads, native desktop and mobile clients, tasks, SMS and WhatsApp, and a lower per-user price, with less automation and weaker service level management; for a small team that deliberates over messages, Missive is often the better fit. Help Scout is an email-first shared inbox with a well-regarded knowledge base and a humane product philosophy, simpler and cheaper, without Hiver's Gmail-native architecture. Crisp, Tidio, Intercom and tawk.to are chat-first platforms that add email, and Intercom in particular leads on artificial intelligence agents and product engagement at premium pricing. Zendesk, Freshdesk, Freshservice and Zoho Desk are ticketing-led help desks with workforce management, governance, self-service depth and enterprise controls; they are stronger for a large support operation and impose a ticket abstraction that Gmail-native teams resist. Gorgias is commerce-led and very strong for Shopify stores. Kustomer is CRM-led. Chatwoot and FreeScout are open-source and self-hostable, with FreeScout notable as a low-cost self-hosted shared inbox. Superhuman is an individual email client. Hiver's position is unique: the only substantial help desk that keeps the team in Gmail while adding assignment, statuses, service levels, automation, knowledge base, voice, WhatsApp, chat, AI assistance and CRM synchronisation.

Pricing is paid per user with a free trial and no permanent free plan. Subscription is billed per user per month or per year at a discounted annual rate, and tiers are differentiated by service level agreements, automation depth, voice and WhatsApp channel availability, artificial intelligence features, reporting, knowledge base capability, integrations, security controls and support level. Enterprise arrangements are quote-based and add governance, single sign-on, audit logging and contractual terms. Because Google Workspace is a prerequisite for the Gmail-native experience, total cost includes the Workspace subscription a company is probably already paying, and buyers should compare per-seat cost against Front and Missive on total rather than on headline price. Current figures are published on the vendor pricing page.

The limitations should be stated plainly. The Gmail dependency is both the appeal and the constraint: a team on Microsoft 365 or on another mail system cannot use the core experience as designed, which excludes a large share of the market. The interface is Gmail, so anything Gmail cannot express, Hiver cannot either, and the visual and interaction ceiling is set by Google rather than by the vendor. Automation is shallower than Front's and ticketing is less structured than Zendesk's or Freshdesk's, so a large support operation with complex routing, workforce scheduling and lifecycle requirements will outgrow it. Analytics are adequate for a small team and insufficient for operational modelling at scale. Enterprise governance and compliance depth are less mature than at the leaders. Adding an extension layer over Gmail introduces occasional friction with other Gmail add-ons, browser extensions and Google's own interface changes, which is an inherent risk in the architecture. And artificial intelligence drafting requires human review to be safe.

Hiver fits teams already on Google Workspace working shared Gmail addresses, startups and small businesses whose support is email-first and whose team will not adopt a new interface, finance and operations teams handling billing, invoicing and vendor email collaboratively, recruitment teams coordinating candidate correspondence in a shared inbox, agencies and professional services firms managing client email with service level expectations, businesses in markets where WhatsApp is a primary customer channel, and companies that want help desk discipline without a migration project. It does not fit organisations on Microsoft 365 or other mail systems, large support teams needing workforce management and deep ticketing, companies requiring complex rule-based routing across many departments, enterprises with strict governance and audit requirements, product-led businesses whose support happens in-app, or teams for whom Missive or Help Scout would deliver most of the value at a lower price.

In the closing comparison, choose Hiver when your team lives in Gmail and you need assignment, statuses, service levels, automation, a knowledge base and additional channels without asking anyone to learn a new interface. Choose Front when you need deeper routing, broader channels and stronger analytics and are willing to move email into a dedicated platform. Choose Missive when internal chat in threads, native applications and a lower per-user price matter more than service level rigour. Choose Help Scout when email-first support with an excellent knowledge base and a simple product suits a small team. Choose Zendesk or Freshdesk when ticketing depth, self-service and workforce management are the requirements. Choose Gorgias when you run a Shopify store. Choose Intercom when artificial intelligence agents and conversational support are the priority. The decisive question for Hiver is whether Gmail is where your team already works; if it is, Hiver removes the largest obstacle to support tool adoption, which is people not using the tool, and that is worth more than any feature comparison.
